entries.section: (1) John the Baptist and the Baptism of Christ

paragraphs.text: St. Matthew and St. Luke referred to some of the events connected with the bodily birth of Christ, and St. John referred to the divine birth of the Son from the Father. St. Mark, however, took a direct approach, declaring in his very first words that his book is the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and he focused on the beginning of Christ's ministry, without mentioning any events that preceded it.
"Jesus": its meaning is "God saves"; its Hebrew origin is Yehoshua, which developed into Yeshua, and then "Jesus." This was the name of the Lord in His incarnation.

"Christ": that is, the One anointed as King, who is set apart for the salvation and renewal of mankind through its redemption on the Cross. "Son of God": that is, the name of divinity, which indicates the Godhead of the Word, the Son of God.

entries.section: (1) John the Baptist and the Baptism of Christ

paragraphs.text: "As it is written": St. Mark refers to the prophecies (Mal 3:1; Isa 40:

3) in the Old Testament, which pointed to the sending of John the Baptist as a messenger going before Christ the Savior, preparing souls to receive Him. In the Roman era, it was necessary for rulers or prominent persons to be preceded by someone who announced their coming. The world, in its corruption, was not ready to receive Christ, so God sent John to rebuke and to warn of the need for repentance, in order to prepare the way for Him.
"I send ... My messenger": the expression that Malachi used in his prophecy about John the Baptist.
"The voice of one crying": the expression that Isaiah used in his prophecy about John the Baptist, and it shows his crying out against evil and the wicked, calling for repentance.

entries.section: (1) John the Baptist and the Baptism of Christ

paragraphs.text: The work that John did was to call people to repentance and to the forsaking of sin. It was the custom of the Jews to circumcise those among the Gentiles who converted to Judaism. In this way John changed that custom, and he used Baptism as a sign and a seal for the one who offered repentance (water being a symbol of washing and purity). The people responded to the call to repentance, and they went out to him from all places, and they were baptized.

entries.section: (1) John the Baptist and the Baptism of Christ

paragraphs.text: "Camel's hair": a coarse, cheap garment worn by the poor, and worn also by the prophets, such as Elijah. It signifies detachment and the absence of love of money and its luxury.
"A girdle of a skin": as Elijah also wore (2 Kgs 1:8). It is a wide leather belt that tightens the waist, and it signifies striving and diligent work.

"He did eat locusts and wild honey": ... The locust is the well-known gnawing insect of the wilderness, and eating it was not forbidden (Lev 11:22), and the honey was the honey of bees found in the clefts of the rocks in the wilderness. Symbolically, it may be said that the locusts resemble the Jews who fell like insects in their sins, whereas repentance makes them sweet honey to Christ.

entries.section: (1) John the Baptist and the Baptism of Christ

paragraphs.text: Besides his powerful call to repentance, he preached and prophesied about the coming of Christ. In humility, he made clear the difference between the two of them, placing himself in the position of the bent servant who loosens with his hand the thongs of his master's sandals. So the Lord lifted up that hand and placed it on His head at the Baptism, to teach us all that humility is the virtue that raises a person before God ... John also did not forget to make clear the difference between the baptism of water, which signifies cleansing, and the baptism of the Holy Spirit, which is founded on Christ.
My beloved friend, we cannot leave the figure of John without learning much from him:

First: he left the comfortable world for the desolate wilderness, which signifies evil, so that evil might be overcome by the call to repentance. Second: he was detached in his food, his drink and his clothing, so God gave him a peace, strength and courage that the world had not known. Third: despite his bold and powerful words, and his refusal to compromise with evil and his rebuking of the wicked, the crowds went out to him. So never be afraid to hold fast to the truth, whatever the evil around you, for it is God who works in you, and not we ourselves.

entries.section: (1) John the Baptist and the Baptism of Christ

paragraphs.text: At the time appointed beforehand by God, Christ went to John at the river Jordan, to be baptized on behalf of sinful mankind, and not out of any need for repentance or cleansing.
"Nazareth of Galilee": the northern part of the land of Judea, and it is the place where Christ spent the days of His life from His return from Egypt as a child until the beginning of His preaching.

"Coming up out of the water": a clarification that Christ went down and came up, and for this reason our Church practices the sacrament of Baptism by immersion, and not by putting water on the head of the one being baptized; and the word "coming up" points to the resurrection from sin through Baptism.

"The heavens opened": the Baptism of Christ was accompanied by a declaration from heaven, and it was the first clear declaration to mankind of the doctrine of the Most Holy Trinity: the incarnate Son comes up from the water, the Holy Spirit takes the form of a dove and reveals Himself, and here is the Father declaring His eternal relationship with His Son, and that He is well pleased with His redemption of mankind. For this reason our Church considers the Feast of Epiphany a great feast of the Lord, and calls it by its theological name, "the Feast of the Divine Manifestation," because it is the declaration of the Most Holy Trinity.

entries.section: (2) The temptation in the wilderness and the beginning of the preaching

paragraphs.text: In a clear indication of the Spirit's leading of the Christian after Baptism, the Lord went out into the wilderness of temptations, so that the believer may learn that the spiritual life will not be free of battles, but that we must overcome through Christ, as He overcame Satan. And despite the wild beasts, which signify the demons in their number and the variety of their warfare, the angels of the Lord minister to and guard His children who strive in His person. In this way God surrounds His Church with His care and concern, which keeps us and comforts us in our trials.

It is noted that St. Mark did not present the details of the spiritual battles throughout the forty days, but both Matthew and Luke spoke, in the fourth chapter of their Gospels, about the details of three of them, as an example of what Christ was exposed to of these battles.

entries.section: (2) The temptation in the wilderness and the beginning of the preaching

paragraphs.text: "Now after that John was put in prison": that is, after Herod imprisoned John the Baptist, who used to oppose his evil by rebuking him, Christ began His ministry in Galilee, north of Judea (Nazareth and Capernaum), where He was first raised. In His wisdom, He did not begin in Jerusalem, so as not to clash with Herod or the chief priests. "The time is fulfilled": that is, the time had come for the fulfillment of all the prophecies written about Him in His incarnation and His redemption of man (Gen 49:10; Dan 9:24).

"The kingdom of God is at hand": that is, the beginning of the call to salvation and the clear manifestation of the glory of God, for the long-awaited Christ had come, and it is for man to declare his acceptance of this call through repentance and belief in the gospel of Christ. My Lord, my God and my Savior, You still call me to be Your son, to inherit the kingdom of life, and You laid down a condition for my obtaining it, which is my abiding always in repentance...
I beseech You, my God, give me also a repentant heart, steadfast in this repentance, for I do not want to lose my inheritance...

entries.section: (3) The calling of some disciples and the healing of a demoniac in Capernaum

paragraphs.text: "The sea of Galilee": it is the same as the Sea of Tiberias and the Lake of Gennesaret, and it forms the eastern border of the land of Galilee.

"Simon and Andrew": fishermen, that is, from the simple folk, for God does not want the success of the ministry to be attributed to man's abilities, but to His own work through the simple, humble servant.

Their two names signified qualities that qualify a person for the service of God: Simon means the one who listens and obeys the word of God, and Andrew means "truly a man" ... that is, manliness and spiritual seriousness in service. "Come ye after me": that is, following Christ and imitating Him in all His attributes and teachings, for the faithful and influential servant is the one who makes Christ the leader of the whole course of his life, so that he takes from Him first in order to give to others second.
"They forsook their nets": their response was immediate, and they left whatever hindered them from following Christ, and this response means the following:
Their faith in Christ, their love for Him, their readiness to leave everything for His sake.

entries.section: (3) The calling of some disciples and the healing of a demoniac in Capernaum

paragraphs.text: The same situation is repeated with James, whose name means "he who follows closely," pointing to the striving and struggle of the servant, and with John, whose name means "God is gracious to His creation." As Simon and Andrew did, they left their father in the ship with the hired servants, and went after Him, which indicates that they were among the wealthy who employed hired servants in fishing.

My dear friend, are you not ashamed with me before those who left everything to follow the good part? What then do we leave in this world for the sake of God? Let us begin with the least things, and God is able to set us over more afterward.

entries.section: (3) The calling of some disciples and the healing of a demoniac in Capernaum

paragraphs.text: Capernaum was one of the largest cities of Galilee on the shore of the sea, and the synagogue was the place of worship where the Jews gathered for prayer and for the reading of the books of Moses and some of the prophecies. Synagogues were spread throughout the land of Judea, but there was only one temple, in Jerusalem, in which sacrifices were offered. "He taught": that is, He read some of the readings, and then gave the interpretation and the exhortation. His teaching was new, carrying spiritual influence and authority over those who listened, unlike the scribes, whose task was to teach and exhort the people at that time.

"The scribes": they trace their descent to Ezra the scribe, who is the most famous of those who collected and copied the holy books after some of the people returned from the captivity to Jerusalem, and the Book of Ezra was written in his name.

entries.section: (3) The calling of some disciples and the healing of a demoniac in Capernaum

paragraphs.text: Present with the crowd in the synagogue was a man possessed by Satan, who could not bear the words of Christ, and who recognized His blessed person, and cried out in great alarm: I know You, You are the Holy One, the Son of God, in whose hand alone is the authority to destroy us.

"And Jesus rebuked him": that is, He reproved him firmly, and commanded him to be silent and to come out of this man. This shows the absolute authority of the Lord Christ over the whole kingdom of evil and of the demons, and that Christ does not accept testimony from Satan even if it is true, for there is no fellowship of light with darkness.

entries.section: (3) The calling of some disciples and the healing of a demoniac in Capernaum

paragraphs.text: In Satan's last desperate attempts, he threw the man down in a faint, but he could do nothing but come out and obey the command of Christ. The coming out of this demon had a profound effect on those who watched from among the crowd, so they marveled, asking about the person of Christ Himself, "What is this?" Then they marveled also at the manner of His teaching, at which they were astonished and had never heard the like before, and finally they were amazed at His authority over the unclean spirits, the like of which they had never seen, as they saw the demon come out at one word from His mouth.
And of course this event had a great effect, so its report spread, not only in Capernaum, but in all the villages of the region of Galilee and the surrounding area.

entries.section: (4) The healing of Peter's mother-in-law and the preaching in the cities of Galilee

paragraphs.text: "The house of Simon and Andrew": Christ came out of the synagogue and went with the four disciples to the house of Simon and his brother Andrew, and this house was in Capernaum, and some hold that the house of Simon Peter was the one where Christ always stayed when He visited Capernaum.

entries.section: (4) The healing of Peter's mother-in-law and the preaching in the cities of Galilee

paragraphs.text: Simon's mother-in-law, who lived with him, had been taken with a great fever. When they told Him of this, He had compassion on her and raised her up, taking her by the hand. In this regard St. Luke says (4:39), "He rebuked the fever, and it left her: and immediately she arose and ministered unto them."
And this, beloved, teaches us two things:

(1) That we ask of Christ not only for our own illnesses, but we also pray for the sufferings of others, as the household of Simon's mother-in-law did, and as the Church teaches us when she prays for the sick in all her prayers. (2) That the woman, when she was healed, offered thanks by serving everyone. So thanking God is not words only, but deeds also.

entries.section: (4) The healing of Peter's mother-in-law and the preaching in the cities of Galilee

paragraphs.text: "At even, when the sun did set": ... out of respect for the commandment of the Sabbath and not traveling during it, the people waited until the Sabbath ended with the setting of the sun, and then gathered around the house, desiring the healing of their sick, or to see the miracles of healing, and healing was accomplished for great numbers, as was also the casting out of unclean spirits.
"He suffered not the devils to speak": ... Christ always did so, because He does not accept testimony about Himself from Satan (see v. 25).

entries.section: (4) The healing of Peter's mother-in-law and the preaching in the cities of Galilee

paragraphs.text: "In the morning ... a solitary place": that is, at the dawn of Sunday, before anyone had risen ... and the purpose of the solitary place was that no one should see or hear Him.
Christ teaches us and gives us a model of quiet prayer in which a person is alone with God, and withdraws with Him to speak with Him and rejoice in meeting Him.
And if Christ, my friend, being without sin, prays ... how much more do we need, we who are burdened with sins and cares, to stand before God to obtain our rest?!

entries.section: (4) The healing of Peter's mother-in-law and the preaching in the cities of Galilee

paragraphs.text: Because of Christ's absence from the house when the four disciples awoke, they searched for Him. And when they found Him, they told Him that there were many people seeking Him (in Capernaum). But Christ, who came forth from heaven for the preaching and the proclaiming of the Kingdom, let nothing hinder Him, so He told the disciples that He must go to the surrounding villages to complete His work.

And here we learn from the Lord Christ a useful lesson, which is that we should not let crowding or insistence make us forget our spiritual goals, for how many hindrances we shall meet ... so do not allow them, beloved, to turn your gaze away from your spiritual work or your eternity.

entries.section: (4) The healing of Peter's mother-in-law and the preaching in the cities of Galilee

paragraphs.text: At first Christ was permitted to enter the synagogues of the Jews in Galilee, but on His later visits, after the slanders of the priests and the leaders of the Jews, He was forbidden to preach and teach in the synagogues. It is noted thereby that faith in Him, after the acceptance of His teaching in the synagogues, was what cast out the demons ... for faith always precedes healing.

The leprous man came worshiping the person of Christ with respect and humility. Despite his hope and his need for healing, he teaches us an important lesson in how to ask of God, for he knelt and said to Him: "If thou wilt," that is, "Let Your will be done."
Despite our confidence in God's ability to answer all our requests, we must put the will of Christ above our need, because He knows what is right and best for us.

"Moved with compassion ... and touched him": St. Mark reveals to us the disposition of the heart of Christ, filled with tenderness toward His creation, for although the word of Christ alone was enough to heal him, He touched him with His hand, a feeling of which this man had been deprived, since the Law forbade touching a leper because of his uncleanness. So the touch of the hand came tenderly upon this body, which had forgotten the meaning of being gently patted by another for a long time. And at the moment in which Christ said "I will," the leprosy departed from him and he was cleansed.
And this teaches us that when we feel aversion toward some person, we should remember the tenderness of Christ toward the leper, and His tenderness toward us sinners.

"And He straitly charged him": what is meant is not rebuking the man, upon whom He had had compassion, but rather that He obliged him not to return to the sin that had been the cause of his illness, and also obliged him to go to the priest, who, according to the Law, examines and declares the healing, and receives the sacrifices that he must offer.

And it is noted here that although the healing was completed, Christ respected the order that God had established, and the role of the priest in it, as it is stated in the Book of Leviticus (chs. 13, 14), that when a leper was healed, he had to go to the priest for examination, and then offer a thank offering in the temple.

Likewise we can say that this is what happens in the sacrament of repentance and confession: the person comes to Christ kneeling and acknowledging his sins, and He says to him: I take them away from you. But go and show yourself to the priest, and offer there the sacrifice of your confession.
"See thou say nothing to any man": that is, do not boast of your healing, claiming that your righteousness was the cause of it, but keep your humility.

May we, my beloved brother, learn to surround God's private dealings with us with some care and secrecy, lest we be afflicted with pride and conceit ... and make your father of confession your reference in this.

But the man, because of his great joy and excitement, spread the news of his healing in all places, until the fame of the Lord Jesus spread in the surrounding country, and He was not able to enter it because of the crowding, so He stayed in the desert places so that everyone could meet Him.
The healing of the paralytic, the calling of Matthew, and confrontations with the scribes and Pharisees

entries.section: (1) The miracle of the healing of the paralytic

paragraphs.text: Capernaum was the center that Christ used during His preaching in Galilee, so He would go out from it to the villages and return to it. As for the house referred to, many hold that it was the house of the Apostle Peter. When He entered, the house became crowded, and there was no longer room for anyone. And instead of taking some rest after being away for days, Christ began to teach the crowd inside the house.

My Lord ... You knew no rest throughout the journey of Your incarnation, in order to give us rest by Your words, Your teaching and Your redemption ... Teach us also to labor for the sake of others, breaking the prisons of our selfishness, and to seize every opportunity to speak of You with others.

entries.section: (1) The miracle of the healing of the paralytic

paragraphs.text: "Palsy": that is, paralyzed.
"Borne of four": that is, his paralysis covered his whole body.
And the four men point to the four Gospels, which carry the sinner (the paralytic) to Christ, or they represent the Church, which, by the intercession of her prayers, carries sinners to repentance.

Because of the crowd, and their inability to get through to Christ, they went up onto the roof of the house (which was covered with wooden boards and some branches), and broke it up, that is, they were able to open a place in it, and let down the paralytic with his bed before Christ by means of ropes.

entries.section: (1) The miracle of the healing of the paralytic

paragraphs.text: Christ marveled at their faith and their striving, with its perseverance and toil, and said to the paralytic: "Son (that is, He restored to him his sonship), thy sins be forgiven thee." Thus He granted him spiritual healing before bodily healing, whereas in the healing of the paralytic at the pool of Bethesda, the Lord granted him bodily healing first, because he was despairing and broken, and had no one (Jn 5:5-9).
And this teaches us that God, in His love for us, deals with each of us according to his need.

entries.section: (1) The miracle of the healing of the paralytic

paragraphs.text: The scribes, the teachers of the Law who were present in the house, condemned Christ for His saying and considered it blasphemy.
"Blasphemies": blasphemy is everything that offends God or His Law, for who can forgive sins but God alone? Consequently, the blasphemy here is the claim of divinity.

entries.section: (1) The miracle of the healing of the paralytic

paragraphs.text: "Perceived in His spirit": that is, He knew by His divinity, being the Searcher of hearts and thoughts, and for this reason He surprised them with His knowledge of what was within them, and asked them: Which is easier, to say to the man, "Thy sins be forgiven thee," or to command him to take up his bed and walk? Christ was not waiting for an answer, but wanted to declare to them that He alone has authority over spiritual healing and bodily healing, by forgiving sins and raising up from a hopeless illness.

entries.section: (1) The miracle of the healing of the paralytic

paragraphs.text: The forgiveness of sins is a hidden spiritual work that man cannot see, and consequently it is possible to doubt whether they have really been forgiven, or whether this one who forgives is a blasphemous and misleading man, whose claim cannot be proved. For this reason the Lord commanded the paralytic to arise, take up his bed and return to his household, which is the work they thought to be the harder! So Christ, besides the miracle of healing, gave the scribes the practical proof of His authority to forgive.

"Immediately he arose": that is, at once, and without help from anyone, and he went out walking, so that all who were in the house and outside it were amazed, and they gave glory to God and to His blessed name, confessing that in all their lives they had never seen or heard the like of this.
The sight of the four friends still stands before our eyes, for they are an example of self-giving and sacrificial service for the sake of others.

You may not, my friend, have a regular service in the Church. But are you at least careful to carry the members of your household to Christ, or to bring Christ to them through your conversation, your prayer, or your reading of the Holy Bible with them?
Be careful, beloved ... for if you do not plant Christ in them, the world will plant its poisons in them.

entries.section: (2) The calling of Matthew and his feast

paragraphs.text: After the miracle, Christ went out of the house, fleeing from the glorification of men, to the sea.

And when the crowds followed Him, He continued His work of teaching them. And as He walked along, He met St. Matthew, who, like many of the Jews, bore two names, one of them Levi the son of Alphaeus, and he was sitting at the place of receipt of custom (the collecting of taxes), which he collected harshly from the Jews, and for this reason the tax collectors (publicans) were hated by the whole Jewish people: first, for their harshness; second, because they worked for the benefit of the Romans, the occupiers. While he was sitting, Christ called him, and he responded at once, and left everything he had been doing, and arose and followed Him.

How great is Your heart, my God ... You call sinners and tax collectors to enjoy life with You and to serve Your holy name. But the difference is the measure of our readiness to leave what occupies us away from You.
Grant us, O God, to set aside for You a time and a place ... and to leave behind us the place where we collect our tolls.

entries.section: (2) The calling of Matthew and his feast

paragraphs.text: In his astonishment, and in his disbelief at the Lord's choosing him, Matthew made a feast in his house and invited to it his friends from among the tax collectors and others, that they might come to know Christ. But the scribes and the Pharisees, who had begun to watch and pursue the Lord and to criticize His actions, did not like this gathering, so they addressed their words to His disciples: How can your Teacher sit with these unclean people?!
But the Lord, when He heard this speech, answered them, making clear the following spiritual truths: (1) that Christ is the Physician who heals our spiritual illnesses, our sins, and none other.

(2) That God does not hate the sinner, but is ready even to sit with him and speak with him for the purpose of saving his soul. (3) That those who feel their spiritual illnesses are the ones who obtain healing, repentance and forgiveness. But the proud, and those who consider themselves healthy, gain nothing from Christ.

entries.section: (3) Christ's answers to the questions of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: Spiritual zeal moved the disciples of John, and indignation moved the Pharisees, and both groups kept the Jewish fasts, and they asked Christ, with some reproach or fault-finding, about the reason His disciples did not fast. In the verses that follow (vv. 19-22), He explained His answer with three illustrative examples, which are the parable of the wedding, the parable of the cloth, and the parable of the keeping of wine, and each of them had its own purpose and explanation (see also Mt 9:14-17).

entries.section: (3) Christ's answers to the questions of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: The parable of the wedding: Christ did not abolish the idea of fasting, but He made clear that it is a means of being with Him at His wedding. And since He was the Bridegroom in the midst of His disciples during His incarnation, there is no need for fasting while the wedding continues. But when He is taken from them by His ascension, fasting will be required of them.

entries.section: (3) Christ's answers to the questions of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: The parable of the cloth: another comparison, by which Christ meant the difference between the fasts of the Law and the literal and outward ordinances of the Jews, "an old garment," that is, an ancient garment, and the spiritual fasts with the "new piece," that is, the new heart; and it is not possible to join the two together, lest "the rent is made worse," since new cloth usually shrinks after washing, and so tears the old cloth and increases its damage.

entries.section: (3) Christ's answers to the questions of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: The parable of the keeping of wine: a third parable, meaning that new practices need a new spiritual nature, for one who has lived practicing his fasts outwardly all his life cannot bear or understand the requirements of spiritual fasting.
"Bottles": the singular is "bottle" (zikk), and these are skin vessels (waterskins) in which wine or water or any liquid is put. "New wine": that is, the new spiritual practice.
"Old bottles": that is, ancient ones, referring to man before the renewal of his nature.

"New bottles": that is, the new spiritual nature granted to us by Baptism and the Holy Spirit. Therefore new wine, which increases in volume with the passing of time, is not put into old skins that have already stretched, or else the wine is spilled and the skins are ruined.
And symbolically, the three preceding parables may point to the effect of the New Testament upon the Old Testament through the life renewed by the Christian faith.

And the conclusion, beloved ... may we examine ourselves with a specific question: how do we fast ... how do we pray? For God wants prayer, fasting and prostration in spirit, and not by force of habit ... for fasting in the Old Testament was a deprivation of the body ... but in the New Testament it is a liberation of the spirit.
So have you examined yourself beforehand and answered?!

entries.section: (3) Christ's answers to the questions of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: The Pharisees observed a new case against the disciples, for as they were walking through the fields, because of hunger, they plucked ears of wheat to eat their grains. Although the Jewish Law permitted this to any hungry person passing through a field (Lev 19:10), and although eating itself was not forbidden on the Sabbaths, what provoked the Pharisees was the plucking of the ears, for they considered it a work that was not lawful to do on the Sabbath.

entries.section: (3) Christ's answers to the questions of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: When the Lord noticed the Pharisees lying in wait for His disciples, He began His words with some rebuke, "Have ye never read?", meaning: are you ignorant of the Scriptures, you who are the proclaimers of knowledge?! And He reminded them of the deed of David and his men in the days of their flight from King Saul, and how they entered the tabernacle of meeting and ate of the showbread, which none but the priests eat, because of their great hunger, and that the Lord did not count that as sin (1 Sam 21:1-6).

entries.section: (3) Christ's answers to the questions of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: Here Christ came to the conclusion of the intended teaching ... that when God ordained the Sabbath, the Sabbath was not the goal, but the goal was man's rest on this Sabbath. So which has meaning to God: the day or man? By this Christ wanted to correct the narrow conceptions to which people had become accustomed, so that they practiced customs without understanding God's purpose in them.

entries.section: (3) Christ's answers to the questions of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: A bold and clear declaration in which Christ declares of Himself that He is God, the Lord of the Sabbath and the Creator of time ... and the Pharisees did not understand what He meant by that.

"The Son of man": an expression that Christ often used of Himself, pointing to His incarnation and becoming man. Chapter 3: the healing of the withered hand, the choosing of the Apostles, the opposition of some

entries.section: (1) The healing of the man with the withered hand

paragraphs.text: The preaching was still in Galilee, and this synagogue was in one of its cities. When the Lord entered, as was His custom, to teach, there was there a man with a paralyzed hand, and St. Luke adds that it was his right hand. Everyone watched Him, especially His enemies, to see whether He would break the law of keeping the Sabbath and heal this man, so that they might bring a complaint against Him for doing the miracle!

entries.section: (1) The healing of the man with the withered hand

paragraphs.text: Christ asked the man to stand forth in the midst, either to stir their feelings of mercy and compassion toward the sick man, or so that the sick man might be in a distinguished place where everyone could clearly see the work of God. "Is it lawful on the sabbath days": Christ knew that His enemies were lying in wait for Him, and so, before healing the man, He asked them a question to put them to shame and to rebuke them for the hardness of their hearts, namely whether it is lawful to do good or to do evil on the Sabbath, and everyone kept silent, for they did not know what to answer.

entries.section: (1) The healing of the man with the withered hand

paragraphs.text: The hardness of heart in their not answering Christ showed their evil, which angered the Lord with a holy anger, so He commanded the man to stretch out his hand, and he stretched it out at once and it was freed from its paralysis. It is noted that Christ's anger was against the sin of hardness of heart, and was free from evil, and was mixed with grief for the sinners, for Christ did not intend by His anger any harm to those with whom He was angry.
Instead of becoming angry, try to find solutions, and do not make the problem more complicated and tear people down.

entries.section: (1) The healing of the man with the withered hand

paragraphs.text: "The Herodians": a political group of the Jews belonging to Herod the Great, who sided with the emperor of Rome out of desire for power, and there was great enmity between them and the Pharisees, but they united in enmity against Christ and in getting rid of Him, though the motive of each was different, and what they took counsel about shows the evil that was in their hearts.

The right hand always signifies man's strength, but sin turns strength into weakness, and puts all of us into some state of paralysis and stiffness ... So command me, O God, to stretch out my hand and be freed from the fetters of my weakness, so that shame is turned into boasting and weakness into strength and victory in Your holy name.

entries.section: (2) The multitudes follow Him and many are healed

paragraphs.text: Pointing to the growth of Christ's fame because of His teaching and His miracles, St. Mark makes clear that those who followed Christ came from every quarter.
"Galilee": the north of the country, where He was preaching.
"Judaea": the southern part of the country, whose capital is Jerusalem.
"From Jerusalem": that is, the followers were not from the villages of Judea, but the meaning is that the fame of Christ had reached the religious capital.
"Idumaea": it lies in the far south of the country, and its name comes from Edom (Esau).
"Beyond Jordan": that is, east of the river.
"Tyre and Sidon": outside the land of Judea, which means that those who followed Christ were not Jews only, but Gentiles also.
And the motives of those who followed Him were many, for some followed Him out of curiosity, or seeking healing, or to hear His teaching, or to know His true identity, or to accuse Him.

entries.section: (2) The multitudes follow Him and many are healed

paragraphs.text: As the crowding increased, and as the sick were eager to touch Him for healing from their diseases, the Lord asked the disciples to find a small ship (a boat) to wait on Him, so that He might enter it and teach the crowds from it, as He often did.

entries.section: (2) The multitudes follow Him and many are healed

paragraphs.text: Those afflicted by unclean spirits would submit to Him, and the evil spirits came out crying out from His divine authority. But Christ asked and commanded these spirits not to mention His name, for He does not like the wicked to bear witness to Him.

entries.section: (3) The choosing of the twelve Apostles

paragraphs.text: (See also the commentary on Mt 10:1-4; Lk 6:13).

St. Luke makes clear (6:13) that the night before the calling of the disciples was spent by Christ in prayer, to teach us that the choosing of servants is a great responsibility, which should not be undertaken without prayer and seeking God's guidance.

"And calleth unto him whom he would": it makes clear that the calling of servants is a divine calling, and not according to a human purpose. And God uses His Church and those who call in her in choosing His servants.

"And he ordained twelve": from a large number of His disciples, the Lord chose twelve disciples for the purpose that "they should be with him": that they accompany Him always, and learn from Him and watch, in order to bear witness to the whole world by their preaching. "Power": given directly by Him to heal and to cast out demons, and even to forgive sins, as it is stated in (Jn 20:23).

entries.section: (3) The choosing of the twelve Apostles

paragraphs.text: The Lord Jesus changed the names of some of the disciples, as He did in ancient times in changing the names of those He chose, such as Abram and Sarai, who became "Abraham and Sarah" (Gen 17:5, 15). A name has importance in a person's life, since it makes clear his mission in service ... So Simon received the name Peter, that is, the rock in faith, and likewise James the son of Zebedee and John, the Lord gave them the name Boanerges, which is a Syriac word meaning the sons of thunder, for they became strong in the Spirit like the heavenly beings.

entries.section: (3) The choosing of the twelve Apostles

paragraphs.text: As for the rest of the disciples and the meanings of their names, they are as follows:
"Andrew" (truly a man), and he was a fisherman like his brother Peter.
"Philip" (the lamp), born in Bethsaida, and he is different from the deacon Philip in (Acts 6:5).

"Bartholomew" (son of the one attached to the water), and he is the same as Nathanael, as was the custom of many of the Jews, who bore two names. "Matthew" (gift), and before his choosing he was also called "Levi."
"Thomas" (the depths) or (twin), and he was known for rationality and doubt.

"James the son of Alphaeus" (he who follows closely), called the son of Alphaeus to distinguish him from James the son of Zebedee, the elder, and he has another name, "James the Less," and he is the writer of the Epistle of James.
"Thaddaeus" (he who guards the heart), and he is the brother of James the Less, and is known also by the two names: Lebbaeus and Judas, not Iscariot.
"Simon the Canaanite" (the one who hears), and the title "the Canaanite" means the zealous.
"Judas Iscariot": "Judas" means praise and thanksgiving, and "Iscariot" means (a man of Kerioth), which is a village of the villages of Judea.
"Which also betrayed him": how strange that God chooses a man, and this man does not remain in the honor that God gave him, but his end is destruction!

So let us be careful, my brother, of vain boasting, and do not say that I am chosen of God and assured of salvation ... Yes, God called us by His grace to sonship in Baptism, but we must stand firm and resist the lusts and the love of the world and of money which destroyed this disciple.
"And they went into an house": the Holy Bible did not mention whose house it was, though the nearest of the houses is the house of Peter.

entries.section: (4) The blasphemies of the Jews and the answer to them

paragraphs.text: In the house, because of the crowding of people around Christ and the disciples' preoccupation with organizing, there was no opportunity at all for them to taste food. And some of the Lord's relatives came from Nazareth to Capernaum in order to lay hold on Him, for what they had heard about Him was confused, and they thought He was extreme; the nearest of people to Him did not grasp His true identity until after a period of time. And this reminds us of what Christ said, that Satan is able to raise up enemies against a man from his own household (Mt 10:36).

entries.section: (4) The blasphemies of the Jews and the answer to them

paragraphs.text: As for the scribes, the copyists and teachers of the Scriptures, who came down from Jerusalem, the place of the worship of God, they signify those whose thoughts have descended from the height of heaven to the depths, and they came with a new accusation that Christ works by the power of the prince of the demons, because they could not deny the Lord's miracles and His power and authority over everything. "Beelzebub": one of the titles of Satan, and its meaning is (lord of the flies), and he was one of the greatest gods of the pagan cults, therefore he was called the prince of the demons, and was also called the prince of the unclean spirits who enter some people.

entries.section: (4) The blasphemies of the Jews and the answer to them

paragraphs.text: In these four verses the idea is one, for the Lord Jesus wanted to prove the falsehood of this accusation by giving examples that simple people understand, so that they would not be confused by the opinions of the priests. "And he said unto them": the impossibility of one demon casting out another, for the demons are all one kingdom and one order, so how could it be divided against itself, or resist one another? So also is the case with the members of one household, for Satan is too clever to be divided against himself, lest his kingdom be ruined and come to an end.

entries.section: (4) The blasphemies of the Jews and the answer to them

paragraphs.text: Christ continues His speech to make clear to them the untruth of their claim that He is a partner of Satan, for He entered by His infinite power into the kingdom of strong Satan, and bound him outside to free people from his authority; so how then can He be described as using the prince of the demons to cast out demons?!

entries.section: (4) The blasphemies of the Jews and the answer to them

paragraphs.text: Here the Lord, in His reply to the scribes, moves on to make clear the extent of the evil to which they had come, and the punishment of this evil (see the commentary on Mt 12:31-32), and He told them that any sin or offense God forgives a man through repentance, but their blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, who moves man to repentance, has no forgiveness forever, because they rejected the Spirit of God Himself and refused repentance, and so their fate will be destruction.

entries.section: (4) The blasphemies of the Jews and the answer to them

paragraphs.text: Of course, the Spirit who supports Christ is the Holy Spirit, as it is written: "The Spirit driveth him into the wilderness" (ch. 1:12), see also (Mt 4:1; Lk 4:1). Therefore, when the scribes claimed that He had an unclean spirit, they rejected God and the act of repentance, and blasphemed against the Holy Spirit, and this is the cause of their destruction (v. 29).

The holy Virgin Mary came from Galilee, and with her the sons of the maternal aunt of the Lord Christ according to the flesh, and as is commonly known in the region of the Levant, the sons of a maternal aunt are called brothers (as in Upper Egypt, the sons of a paternal uncle are called brothers), and because the house was crowded with people they could not enter, so they sent word by mouth, through the crowd surrounding Christ, asking to see Him.

Christ here moves us from the concept of limited bodily kinship to unlimited spiritual kinship. He of course did not mean to neglect His bodily relatives, He who laid down the commandments, among them the two commandments that are repeated often in both Testaments of the Bible: "Honour thy father and thy mother" (from Ex 20:12 to Eph 6:2), and "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (from Lev 19:18 to Jas 2:8), and He is also the One who entrusted the beloved John with the care of His mother the Virgin at the time of His crucifixion. But the intended meaning is that obedience to God and His commandments creates a spiritual kinship that surpasses the kinship of the flesh among the members of one Church, and makes us the true relatives of God ... And St. John Chrysostom adds to this, saying: "A man becomes a mother to Jesus by preaching Him, for he is like one who begets the Lord in the hearts of his hearers."

What grace You have given me, my God, that You point with Your hand and say of me "Behold my brethren" ... so grant me always to sit at Your feet like those who sat on that day, to learn and grow in the knowledge of You, and to strive with all my strength to fulfill Your will, and to live by Your commandment, that I may become worthy of what You have called me...
The parable of the sower and the mustard seed, the raging of the sea

"By the sea side": this happened more than once, and the sea here is the Sea of Galilee. When the crowd pressed upon Christ, the Lord used one of the fishing boats, and sat in it facing the crowds on the shore to teach them. The sea usually signifies the troubled world, and the salt sea, which makes thirsty everyone who drinks from it, and the ship signifies the Church, the source of teaching and of salvation.

"In parables": one of the methods that the Lord often used in teaching, and there is also direct preaching, like the Sermon on the Mount. Here He uses a pictorial parable connected with the surroundings and the minds of the people, to make easier the meaning intended to be pictured.

"The sower": he is God, and likewise every faithful servant whom God uses in spreading His word (the seed). "Went out": that is, came down and became incarnate for the sake of redemption and the preaching of His word, His seed, some of which fell by the way side and did not sprout, for the fowls of the air came and devoured it up.
It is noted that the Lord Christ will return and explain in detail to His disciples the meaning of this parable and the kinds of ground in verses 14-20.

And some fell among the stones on rocky soil, and the root could not penetrate the rocks, and the plant died after having sprung up quickly, and the sun burned it, especially since its roots could not supply it with water and nourishment.

And some fell into ground that could have yielded fruit, had it not been full of thorns and foreign, useless weeds, which shut out from it the sun and the air, and hindered the roots from growing, so it was choked and died.
The last part of the grain fell on good ground, and yielded varied fruit, some thirty, and some sixty, and some a hundred.

"He that hath ears to hear": an expression that Christ used more than once, and what is meant by it is a call to the listener to listen well, understand and meditate, not only on the literal meaning, but also on the deeper spiritual meaning.

My beloved God ... You were careful that Your word should reach every person so that it might bear its fruit, and for this reason You spoke to all people with every kind of speech so that they might understand ... But what do I do? Why do I not speak with people about You or with Your words, for Your words bring joy and comfort, and understanding them and acting by them is the way to eternity?
Grant me, my God, to speak with Your words instead of my own, and with Your wisdom instead of my understanding, so that there may be comfort for me and for others.

After the crowds departed, and when He was alone with Christ, the twelve, with some of His followers, asked Him about the meaning of the parable, and He was pleased with them because they asked Him in order to know the spiritual meanings. "Unto you it is given": a special gift and grace that God gives to His faithful servants to understand the hidden and symbolic spiritual meanings, so that they may be filled with them first, and then explain them to others, each according to his capacity.

The speech here is a reminder from Christ to His disciples of the prophecy of Isaiah concerning the people who resisted the teaching of the prophet in his time (Isa 6:9-10). What is meant by that is that not everyone who hears, and not everyone who sees, believes the word or understands it, but in many cases does not accept it and resists it, and so man judges himself by that, and does not deserve the forgiveness of sins.

The Lord began to explain the parable to them, and made clear that it is simpler than other parables. And He began by saying that God is the Sower, who is careful to cast His word into the hearts of men, and who is able to change man's nature if man wishes it.

"The way side": they are those with proud hearts, because the wayside is higher than the field, and has no fence to protect it, that is, no care. And from the many people passing over the way, it becomes hard, so it resembles people who allow evil thoughts to enter into them, so that their hearts are hardened and they do not receive the word of God. Then Satan comes and takes away the word, so it bears no fruit at all.
My God ... grant me to be a low and humble field, and not a proud wayside, for Your word knows only the humble heart from which to bring forth fruit.

"Stony ground": land with a thin soil that hides within it hard stones, like the hypocritical hearts that show mercy and hide harshness; it also points to the worship of stones, the idols, instead of God. It is land through which the wooden plow, which signifies the Cross, has not passed to break up its hardness, so that its owners may receive the word. And even if these receive the word of God with joy, this is temporary and unstable, and does not stand up against trials or affliction or persecution.

"Thorns": those sown among thorns are choked by the cares of the world and its vain material concerns, and the anxiety and delusion that accompany this because of riches. And St. Clement of Alexandria says: "Do not blame money, but its misuse."

As for the good ground, they are those who hear and do and bear fruit in graduated measure. It is low (humble) ground, plowed (it carried the Cross), exposed to the sun (that is, it stands before its Christ every day), watered by the Holy Spirit and by His precious Blood ... and we notice the following from this parable:

(1) The word of God is available to all, and it is left to man how far he responds to it, or even rejects it. (2) There are levels of being filled and of meditation on the word of God (the disciples), and there is the level of acceptance and understanding (the crowds), and both are acceptable.

(3) The kinds of bad ground are three and the good are three, and this reminds us of the parable of the wise and foolish virgins (Mt 25:1-13), in that God's call and grace are one for all. But what about your reaction, beloved?!
After explaining the parable to the disciples, Christ continued His speech with a rhetorical question, the purpose of which was to call the disciples to serious preaching work.

"Is a candle brought": the candle is the words of Christ, His explanation and His teaching, with which He lit up the hearts and minds of His disciples. And as they were enlightened, they must enlighten the hearts of others with the same words, and this is a responsibility that falls on us also, so we must not be occupied with the world, which the bushel signifies in hiding the word of God, or grow lazy and lie down on the bed, leaving the work of God, but we must lift it high on the candlestick so that the whole world may be lit up with the teaching of Christ. And the candlestick also signifies the Church, shining in the midst of the dark world, for she is responsible for spreading the teaching of Christ. And let us note that the rite of building churches took care to build minarets (towers) in confirmation of this meaning.

That is, what I have explained to you privately of the mysteries of the Kingdom is not to hide it, but to proclaim it and teach by it, and that is your responsibility ... And because of the importance of the matter, the Lord Christ repeated what He said to the crowds in (v. 9), that if any man has ears to hear, let him hear.

Christ asked His disciples to understand the following truth, namely: the justice of God in the face of the love and labor of His servants. Whoever has offered labor for the spread of the Kingdom and the preaching will receive an added reward, and God gives him here the strength to work. But whoever has no desire to work, even his natural gifts which he did not use will be taken from him here, and he will be punished for his negligence in eternity.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the growing seed and the mustard seed

paragraphs.text: "The kingdom of God": there is a difference between the two expressions "the Kingdom of God" and "the Kingdom of Heaven"...

The Kingdom of Heaven means eternity and what follows the Second Coming of Christ. As for the Kingdom of God, it means two things: the first is the spread of faith on earth and the reign of God over the hearts of people, and the second is the work of God in man for the growth of faith within him (ch. 1:14-15).

"A man": signifies Christ Himself or the faithful servant who conveys the words of Christ, and the seed is the words of God and His teachings and commandments, and the ground is the heart of man or of mankind in general.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the growing seed and the mustard seed

paragraphs.text: "The seed should spring and grow up": a clear reference to the work of the Holy Spirit in the Church and in man, for the Holy Spirit is responsible for spiritual growth in the life of each of us, and for this reason the seed grows in the heart and man responds to it.

"He knoweth not how": of course these words refer to the person of the servant who cast the word of God into the hearts, because the responsibility for growth and fruit-bearing is the responsibility of God Himself and not of the servant, as the Apostle Paul said: "Neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase" (1 Cor 3:7).

entries.section: (3) The parable of the growing seed and the mustard seed

paragraphs.text: "The earth bringeth forth fruit of herself": a reference to the new nature of mankind after Baptism, in that it is responsive to the work of God and inclined to good. And the Lord Christ makes clear to us here that spiritual growth in the life of man is gradual growth, and not an upheaval and change in a moment ... so it begins as a simple plant at the beginning of repentance, and after that ears, that is, good works, and then it becomes wheat, that is, ripe, steadfast fruit, and likewise it is a source of spiritual food for others.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the growing seed and the mustard seed

paragraphs.text: "When the fruit is brought forth": that is, at full ripeness. What is meant is the spread of the Kingdom of God over the hearts of people.
"The sickle": a semicircular knife used in harvesting.

The general meaning: when the time is fulfilled and at the end of the days, God sends His angels, the reapers (Mt 13:39), to gather this fruit, and people are taken to heaven to be judged for their works.

My beloved God ... make me good ground that receives Your word which reaches me, and make me subject to Your Holy Spirit ... for I truly want to grow, and I have nothing but Your work in my life, which I need greatly; establish Your word in me, and occupy my heart with Your love, and make me desire to serve You, and be worthy of Your heavenly Kingdom at Your last coming.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the growing seed and the mustard seed

paragraphs.text: A question that Christ asked, not for the purpose of getting an answer from His listeners, but to show us His care to make the truths of the faith clear with simple examples suited to people's minds.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the growing seed and the mustard seed

paragraphs.text: Christ's speech here is still connected with the previous speech about the growth of the work of God within man's life, and how, although it begins small in the heart, like one mustard seed, which is the least of all seeds, God's care makes it a great tree with boughs and branches, that is, various spiritual virtues, so that souls without shelter find rest within it.

Is this not the Church of God, which appears weak in the eyes of the world? Yet she is the oasis of rest for all who are weary and lost in the world ... So how long, my brother, will you remain a stranger to your Church? Come and take shade, and you will find rest and water and pasture, and your Christ, who awaits you with longing to tend your growth and your fruit-bearing.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the growing seed and the mustard seed

paragraphs.text: According to the capacity of the listeners and their understanding, the Lord would speak in parables and comparisons. But privately, that is, with His disciples in their private sessions, He would explain everything to them.

On the same day on which Christ spoke in parables, He asked the disciples to cross the Sea of Galilee to the east of the Jordan, so the disciples sent away the crowds, and took the Lord, without preparations, as He was, into the ship. The ship here points to the Church, which always carries her Christ within her, with the Apostles around Him, that is, her fathers and servants.

Contrary, violent, opposing winds blew, and they point to the trials and battles to which the soul or the Church is exposed in the world, and the high waves point to the lusts with which Satan tries to fill the soul. And Christ, in all this, did not leave His ship (His Church), but was testing the faith of its servants during the affliction, and showing their weakness and the speed with which they turn to Him. So they awoke Him and reproached Him for neglecting them, instead of asking Him with humility and with confidence in His ability to rescue them.

"He rebuked ... and said": ... Christ spoke to the sea and the wind with the authority of a master over his servants, and commanded them to be silent, and the response was immediate and swift, and there was a great calm.

Christ's words to the disciples were a rebuke and reproach for their lack of faith in the face of hardship, and for the manner of their speech with Him, which was not fitting. And after the calm, a greater fear came into the hearts of the disciples, and they asked one another about His true identity, and gained a new spiritual experience of the power of Christ, whom the winds and the sea and all nature obey.
And we learn from this miracle more than one thing:
(1) That the presence of Christ within the Church does not prevent trials and persecutions from occurring.
(2) That the purpose of trials in general is a test of faith and of trust in the work of God.

(3) God's allowing trials for us is so that we may know our weaknesses, and take refuge in Him, and He rescues us and supports us. (4) That however much boldness there is in our speech with our heavenly Father, it must never be at the expense of respect for the honor of the name of God and awe and fear of Him in our hearts.
Chapter 5: the healing of the demoniac, the healing of the woman with the issue of blood, the raising of Jairus' daughter

entries.section: (1) The healing of the demoniac of the country of the Gadarenes

paragraphs.text: We find an explanation of this miracle in (Mt 8:28-34), and let us note the following:
"The country of the Gadarenes": it is east of the Jordan, and it was a commercial region inhabited by Greeks, and it has another name by which it is known, which is "the country of the Gergesenes."

"A man with an unclean spirit": when Christ reached the east of the Sea of Galilee, two demoniacs who lived in the tombs met Him; St. Mark mentioned one of them, who was the more disturbed and raging, and he also made clear the cause of this condition of his, which is that a demon dwelt in him and controlled his actions.

entries.section: (1) The healing of the demoniac of the country of the Gadarenes

paragraphs.text: "Who had his dwelling among the tombs": a link between Satan and tombs, for the place of Satan is always where death and uncleanness are, and these are the banners of his kingdom. And the speech after this is about the power of Satan and his authority over this soul, so that no one could free him from his authority, or humble this demon and subdue him.

"Always, night and day": a picture of the constant torment suffered by the soul which, by its lusts, has put itself under the authority of Satan, so it knows no way of rest, but adds to the wounding of itself by sins (the stones).

entries.section: (1) The healing of the demoniac of the country of the Gadarenes

paragraphs.text: This man rushed with all his torment toward Christ and worshiped Him, and then the demon cried out, confessing the divinity of the Lord Christ and His truth as the Son of God, and His absolute authority in tormenting him with eternal torment.

entries.section: (1) The healing of the demoniac of the country of the Gadarenes

paragraphs.text: The speech here is Christ's, for He commanded Satan to leave the man. And the reason for Christ's asking the name of the demon was not that it was hidden from Him, but to teach us about the ferocity of Satan and his harshness in possessing the soul, and then the power of His authority over the whole kingdom of demons, however many they may be.

entries.section: (1) The healing of the demoniac of the country of the Gadarenes

paragraphs.text: "And he besought him much": it is not easy for Satan in his pride to declare his defeat, despite his confessing Christ's authority over him, and for this reason he asked not to be sent away out of the country, that is, the place. And because Satan knew that Christ would surely cast him out of the man, he asked instead to enter into a herd of swine, which are among the unclean animals in the law of the Old Testament.

entries.section: (1) The healing of the demoniac of the country of the Gadarenes

paragraphs.text: "Gave them leave": it makes clear to us that however great Satan's power, he can do nothing unless God permits it.

Why did Christ give leave?!: perhaps the reader asks why He allowed Satan to enter the herd of swine, and to drive them wild and push them toward the sea, and about two thousand were drowned, which was the number of the whole herd?! Christ allowed this as a chastisement of the owners of the swine, who had raised them in violation of God's commandment, and sold them at cheap prices that tempted people to buy them ... So Christ's punishment was just against one who violated the Law and made people stumble.

entries.section: (1) The healing of the demoniac of the country of the Gadarenes

paragraphs.text: The herdsmen went out in panic and terror to the owners of the herd, and of course they told everyone they met in the cities and their suburbs, so everyone went out to see and to verify. And when they came to the place where the Lord was, they found the demoniac in a new condition to which they were not accustomed ... calm ... sitting ... in his right mind ... and the crowd who had seen the miracle began to tell it to those who had not seen it. But the owners of the swine, to whom the swine mattered more than the man, were distressed by the loss of the herd, and asked the Lord to leave the place!!

entries.section: (1) The healing of the demoniac of the country of the Gadarenes

paragraphs.text: As gratitude, and out of a sincere desire, the man who had been healed wanted to follow Christ and to go into the ship with Him. But the Lord Christ prevented him, and asked something else of him: first, that he go to his household so that they might be comforted by his return in health ... second, that he bear witness to God and His work in his healing.
And the man obeyed, and began to proclaim and tell all people what Christ had done for him.
"Decapolis": the region east of the Sea of Galilee, of which the country of the Gadarenes was one. See also the commentary on (Mt 4:24-25).

We learn from this man something important, which is that man must submit his will to God and not cling to his own opinion ... We present our desires to our Father, yes, but we leave the choice to Him ... for the man's desire was a blessed desire, which was to be with Christ ... but Christ charged him with another service, and he rejoiced in it, and set out to serve diligently ... So let us also learn not to hold fast to our opinions, and to leave the leading of our lives to the wisdom and choice of our God.

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Jairus and the healing of the woman with the issue of blood

paragraphs.text: "The other side": it is the western side of the sea, to which Christ returned after the miracle of the healing of the demoniac. And as usual, the crowds either followed Him or were waiting for Him on His arrival.

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Jairus and the healing of the woman with the issue of blood

paragraphs.text: "One of the rulers of the synagogue": that is, one of the elders of the Jews of high standing from the religious and social side, and the name Jairus means "enlightened," and he represents the Jew enlightened by the Law, so he believes in Christ and worships Him.

"He besought him greatly": that is, he asked with urgency, which makes clear the bad condition of the daughter on one hand, and the tender fatherhood of Jairus and his desire for her healing on the other, placing his last hopes in Christ's visit to her, and his courteous manner in asking, since he first worshiped Christ, then entreated Him saying: "Come and lay thy hands on her ... that she may live." And when Christ saw these feelings, He went with him. And as usual, the crowds followed Him, thronging. My beloved God ... how sweet are the words that Jairus uttered, "Come." Yes, my Lord, come and lay Your hand on me so that I may be cleansed from my sins and healed of my weaknesses ... come to free me from material things and the love of the world.
My beloved brother ... make this petition that Jairus uttered a prayer between your lips, so that in every feeling of weakness or weariness or distress you say: "Come, my Lord Jesus."

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Jairus and the healing of the woman with the issue of blood

paragraphs.text: On the way to the house of Jairus, Christ met the woman with the issue of blood (see Mt 9:
20), whose condition St. Mark explained in detail as an introduction to the miracle.

"Twelve years": that is, the fullness of the time of her pain and of her psychological suffering besides the bodily, since a woman with a flow of blood was considered unclean and could not approach the temple or perform religious practices; and what also would be the state of a body after bleeding for so long a time as this?!

"Physicians ... spent ... worse": St. Mark continues to draw her picture, for she was in despair after going through the physicians and trying all the medicines, and she was poor since she had spent all her money, and her condition became worse, that is, the pains increased and money and medicine were unable to heal her, pointing to the helplessness of men, with all their capabilities, and the need for Christ the Savior.

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Jairus and the healing of the woman with the issue of blood

paragraphs.text: "When she had heard": her case was like that of many who heard about Christ and His miracles of healing, and not only her need or her despair of healing moved her, but there was also a faith that moved her, for she said within herself: "If I may touch," and it was a simple faith, and it also reveals to us her respect for the commandment of the Law in not touching a person because of her uncleanness, so she took a decision to touch nothing but His clothes.

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Jairus and the healing of the woman with the issue of blood

paragraphs.text: The moment of her touching the clothes of the Savior was the moment of her healing, and she felt a wonderful new power running through her body.

My beloved brother ... do you not ask with me how the woman with the issue of blood was healed without even asking?! It is the simple, humble faith that many have lost in these days!! Her sense of unworthiness made her come from behind Him and be ashamed to ask, and her faith made her press through the crowd, despite the weakness of her body, so she obtained what she wanted. O my God, grant me to be like her in her virtues: believing ... humble ... persevering ... striving.

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Jairus and the healing of the woman with the issue of blood

paragraphs.text: "The virtue had gone out": an expression of the Lord Christ's awareness of what had happened. And the word "gone out" means that He is the one with authority over healing and the giver of it, and not His bare clothes. My beloved brother ... the established tradition in our Church teaches the honoring of the bodies and relics of the saints, and the keeping in our churches of some of their relics ... and people are blessed by touching them and by seeking their intercession for healing or the receiving of a blessing.

And to those who oppose this tradition, we say that the clothes of Christ carried all His power ... so also the relics of the saints carry the power of God Himself, for the Healer in every case is God with His full authority, but He gives honor to the names of His holy children.
"Who touched my clothes?": of course Christ knew who had touched His clothes, but by this question He wanted two things: the second: the proclaiming of the miracle itself to everyone.
The first: the proclaiming of the faith of the humble woman.

But because the disciples did not understand the Lord's purpose, they asked in wonder: Thou seest the multitude thronging thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me?! But Christ continued to look around, giving the woman an opportunity to declare herself.

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Jairus and the healing of the woman with the issue of blood

paragraphs.text: The woman understood well that she was the one meant by Christ's words and no other, and this increased her fear and confusion, but it did not prevent her from coming forward and confessing the truth, for her human weakness did not push her to flee, but she confessed the truth. And Christ's reply to her was reassuring, removing all anxiety, for He praised her faith and made clear that it was the cause of her healing, and blessed her, and commanded for her the continuance of the healing.
My Lord Jesus ... grant me the courage of the woman with the issue of blood, so that I may draw near to You to obtain the lasting healing from my sins.

The return here is to the story of Jairus' sick daughter, after the end of the healing of the woman with the issue of blood ... for on the way of Jairus' return to his house, some people came from his house to tell him of his daughter's death, and that there was therefore no need for Christ to come, for no one imagined that Christ could do anything with death; but Christ intervened in the conversation, and spoke directly with Jairus, and encouraged him, saying to him: "Be not afraid," and He also gave him the only weapon for driving out fear, which is faith.

"And he suffered no man": ... the crowd followed Him to the house of Jairus, but when entering the house, Christ did not allow anyone to enter except Peter and James and John of the disciples, and these three are the ones whom He also took with Him on the Mount of Transfiguration (ch. 9), and likewise in Gethsemane on the night of His crucifixion.

And as is expected in these circumstances, especially because of the young age of the daughter, the grief and weeping and wailing were great, and Christ surprised them with a question and a truth that astonished the crowd and the family. "Why make ye this ado, and weep?": a question that seems strange in such a situation ... and can anything else be done but weep?!

"The damsel is not dead": and this is the truth that cannot be believed, for the death was plain and real, and the crowds were witnesses to it, and can we not tell the difference between sleep and death?!

"They laughed him to scorn": it seems that they wondered at or mocked the words of Christ, since they were sure of the death of the girl, but Christ took her parents with the three disciples, and entered the room where the girl lay.

Christ took the girl by the hand, and called her with the command to arise from her death, and He alone is the One with authority over death. And the phrase "Talitha cumi" was a widespread Syriac expression, which St. Mark took care to mention as Christ pronounced it, and then translated into its meaning: "Damsel, I say unto thee, arise."

"Arose, and walked": that is, she returned to full health, and did not go through a period of convalescence, for example, that is, the resurrection and healing were accomplished, and everyone was amazed with a wondrous amazement, for what had happened was beyond the belief of any mind. "He charged them straitly that no man should know it": such news cannot be kept quiet, for St. Matthew mentioned that: "The fame hereof went abroad into all that land" (9:26). As for Christ's request, its cause was perhaps the desire not to arouse the envy of the rulers against Him, or that people's faith in Him should be from conviction and not from excitement at the miracles ... and He asked that something be given her to eat, and this is also a confirmation that her resurrection was in her real body and not an illusion.

The entering of Christ into the house of Jairus turned grief into joy, and He still stands at the doors of our hearts, and we still want Him to raise up everyone who has died by sin, and to restore joy to the heart instead of gloom and grief ... Open to Him, beloved, speak with Him and tell Him that you need Him to touch you with His hand to raise you up sound in repentance, and to give you to eat of His true Body and Blood, declaring your healing and your resurrection.
Christ's preaching, the preaching of the disciples, the beheading of John, the two miracles of feeding the crowds, the miracle of walking on the water

entries.section: (1) Christ's preaching in His own country

paragraphs.text: "And he went out from thence": that is, from Capernaum, west of the sea and the river Jordan.
"And came into his own country": that is, Nazareth in the north, and it is the place where the Lord spent His childhood and youth until He began to preach.

entries.section: (1) Christ's preaching in His own country

paragraphs.text: "The sabbath day ... the synagogue": the Sabbath was the day of worship, and if a Jew was in Jerusalem he went to the temple, but in the other cities synagogues were spread about, and they are places set apart for worship, prayers, explanation and interpretation, without the offering of sacrifice, for the sacrifices have their place in the temple alone in Jerusalem. "When they heard": St. Mark pointed to the reaction of the people in being amazed at Christ's teaching, new in its concept and powerful in its effect, and also their wondering and asking about the secret of His wisdom and His miracles of healing.

"The carpenter, the son of Mary": a reference to the work that Christ did before the preaching, which is a simple work. They also mentioned His mother, and mentioned the sons of Mary the wife of Clopas, the sister of the Virgin, who were the sons of His maternal aunt, and Jewish custom considers the sons of a maternal aunt to be brothers.

"They were offended at him": that is, they differed over His person. And the cause of the offense was the earlier talk among the people about the person of Christ, for they knew His upbringing and His family, and wondered and scoffed at Him because of what was being spread about His fame and His works.

entries.section: (1) Christ's preaching in His own country

paragraphs.text: "A prophet is not without honour": the Lord used a proverb well known among the Jews, whose meaning is that a person may find honor, standing and welcome abroad more than he finds it among his relatives who despise him.

entries.section: (1) Christ's preaching in His own country

paragraphs.text: "He could there do no": ... "could not" does not mean the inability of Christ or any lack of His power, God forbid, and what is meant by it is that, because of their unbelief, they deprived themselves of the works of the Lord, except a few who obtained healing because of their faith in Him. But Christ did not despair of their ingratitude, but kept going about the places near Nazareth preaching in them. A counsel, beloved ... unbelief prevents and veils the work of God in our lives, and pride prevents the knowing of the humble God.

"By two and two": Solomon the Wise says: "Two are better than one ... for if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow" (Eccl 4:9, 10), and the wisdom of the Lord in this is that each of them should be a support to the other, especially since the disciples were in their first experiences of the work of preaching, and the Lord did not leave them without help, but gave them power over Satan and the casting out of unclean spirits.

The Lord Christ forbade His disciples some things, so that they would not be occupied with anything away from the work with which they were charged, and so that they would experience His divine provision for all they would need of material things during their service. "A staff only": it is the only thing that Christ permitted the disciples, a clear reference to the Cross, which is the strength of help for the servant who is sent.
"Scrip": the bag that a traveler carries to put his things in.
"Bread": that is, food ... for I am the One who will provide this for you.
"Money" (literally, copper): that is, coins.
"Neither put on two coats": that is, being content with little, and with what is absolutely necessary, for God provides the rest of their needs.

"There abide ... till ye depart": that is, not being occupied with moving about and with feasts in many houses, but being content with what is necessary, which is staying in one house and concentrating on proclaiming the gospel and serving only.

This verse makes clear the recompense for man's refusal to accept the word of God that is necessary for his salvation, for the punishment at the judgment, if the refusal continues, which means blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, will be more severe than God's punishment when He burned Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:24).

"Shake off the dust": a well-known custom among the Jews, whose meaning is that these people are not worthy of association or of sharing in anything, not even the dust of their town. And it means that whoever rejects the servants of God rejects God, because the servant here is a representative and ambassador of Christ Himself.

The disciples began their work as Christ had commanded them, so they began with teaching and preaching the Kingdom, making clear that the way is repentance ... and God gave them power and gifts, so they were able to cast out demons, and likewise to heal the sick by prayer and anointing with oil.
"Anointed with oil": the anointing with oil became a sacrament and a tradition in the Church, received from the Fathers the Apostles (see Jas 5:14).

St. Mark speaks here of the reactions of the people and of Herod the king to the preaching of Christ, for some of the people said "That it is Elias," who had gone up to heaven, come down alive once again, and these are his wonders. And others said that He is a prophet by whom God visits His people after the sending of prophets had ceased for hundreds of years. As for Herod, his sense of guilt over the unjust killing of John the Baptist made him say that it is John, risen from the dead, and mighty works are shown in him, and perhaps he has come to take vengeance on me.

Beloved ... this feeling of Herod is the feeling of many of the wicked who sacrificed their peace of heart for the lust of sin ... for lust made him kill, and after that peace left him, for Isaiah says: "There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked" (Isa 57:21). So do not be deceived, my friend, by sin, for its price is heavy on earth and heavier still in eternity.
