St. Mark here explains the story of the killing of John the Baptist from the beginning, and the motives and events that surrounded it, for John, while teaching the crowds and preaching repentance, also rebuked Herod Antipas, the son of Herod the Great who killed the children of Bethlehem, because he had put his brother Philip in prison and taken his brother's wife as his own wife, which made Herod (the son) seize him and imprison him, to be rid of his rebuking.

Jealousy took hold of Herodias, and feelings of rage and anger toward John possessed her, and she wanted to kill him, but the one who prevented her was Herod himself, who, although he had seized him, feared him and respected him, and knew that he was a man of God. And he heard many of his sayings and kept them, and likewise all the works that he did...
And this is the spiritual awe that God puts on the faces of His children before their persecutors, who may possess weapons and authority, but inwardly fear them and respect them.

At a banquet that Herod held in remembrance of his birthday, to which he invited his lords (his ministers), high captains (the chiefs of his army) and chief estates of Galilee (its notables), Salome, the daughter of Herodias, came in and danced, and her dancing was a source of delight and praise for those present. And as exhilaration took hold of Herod, he wanted to reward her, so he spoke with the boasting and pride of the kings of the earth that she should ask whatever she would, even up to half of his kingdom, and he increased in folly when he made his promise to her with an oath, which made going back on it impossible.

Have you seen, my friend, to what drunkenness and lust and the pride of greatness lead?! Do they not lead to folly and impulsiveness and rashness, in which everything is lost, the most important being wisdom?
So take heed, my friend, and let nothing take from you your will, your awareness and your decision.

St. Mark points out here, as St. Matthew also pointed out (14:8), that what the daughter asked was nothing but the carrying out of her mother's wicked desire for vengeance on John, who represented, even in his prison, the voice of the conscience that does not sleep, which the wicked man always wants to silence, and for this reason she asked ... at once the head of John the Baptist on a charger, which adds cruelty and bloodthirstiness also to her character.

The king was sorry, and it was possible for him to go back on his word. But, because of his pride before his guests and what he had sworn, he went on in his error all the more, and sent the executioner to behead John. And this reminds us of Pilate, who, despite the warnings of God, feared for his position, and sent the innocent Christ to the Cross.

My beloved God ... so it is with the chain of evil once it begins, for it continues and grows more inflamed, and leads to what cannot be avoided, for the fire of evil devours everything even if its beginning was a small spark ... I beseech You, my God, keep me from evil and from myself and from my passions, for I am a weak man and I have none but You in whom to take refuge.

In a scene that shows the ferocity of the human soul possessed by evil, Salome the daughter took the severed head and went with it to her mother, to quench her thirst for revenge with this sight. But the faithful disciples of John took his body and prepared it with spices according to the custom of the Jews, and buried it in sorrow and honor.

entries.section: (4) The return of the twelve and the feeding of the five thousand

paragraphs.text: After relating the story of the martyrdom of John the Baptist, St. Mark takes us back to his account of the sending out of the disciples and their return to Christ. It was natural that the first thing the Apostles did was to tell Christ all that they had done. But Christ, in His tenderness and concern for everything, was not distracted by the reports of the service from caring for the bodily and psychological condition of His disciples, so He called them to some rest after the weariness. And since they had forgotten to eat amid their occupations, He did not forget, so He called them to be alone with them away from the crowding of the crowd, and for this reason He took them to a ship, to a quieter place.

What Christ did with His disciples was most gentle and tender ... He cares for everything ... so what of me, who forget many tender feelings amid the crowding of life?! And perhaps this is what people needed from me more than anything else ... Teach me, my Lord, to be like You as far as I am able.

entries.section: (4) The return of the twelve and the feeding of the five thousand

paragraphs.text: But the crowds who were always pursuing Christ saw Him going with His disciples, and ran there quickly, and others came out of the villages and cities and gathered where Christ was sitting with His disciples in the ship. And when Christ looked out from the ship, He saw the very large numbers and had compassion on them, for they were as sheep not having a shepherd, and He began to teach them with various teachings as He did in the Sermon on the Mount. And after a long preaching, many hours, His disciples came to Him, saying:

"This is a desert place": that is, the place is far from habitation and markets and places where food is sold, "and now the time is far passed": a reference to the length of time and the hunger of the crowds...
Then came the suggestion offered by the disciples to solve this problem, which was to send the crowds away so that they might buy what they lacked of food.

entries.section: (4) The return of the twelve and the feeding of the five thousand

paragraphs.text: Christ's answer came as a surprise to the disciples: "Give ye them to eat"!! ... From where, You who know everything, for we do not have food for these ... and if You meant that we should go and buy, we need at least two hundred pennyworth for bread alone ... and this shows that the number was large. And of course the Apostles' question carried a measure of astonishment at Christ's words!! ... and this is an encounter that often happens between God's will and His all-embracing provision, and man's helplessness and his actual limited abilities...

entries.section: (4) The return of the twelve and the feeding of the five thousand

paragraphs.text: "Go and see": of course Christ knew the number of the loaves and fishes, but He charged the disciples with this so that they might make sure for themselves that there was nothing but this small amount. And it seems that they called out to the crowd ... whoever has food, let him bring it, because St. John mentions that a lad brought it. And some hold that the five loaves point to the five books of Moses, and the two fishes to the Old and New Testaments.

Then He commanded the disciples to make the crowd sit down in groups, company by company, to make the distribution easier ... and the disciples did so, so there were groups of a hundred and others of fifty.

entries.section: (4) The return of the twelve and the feeding of the five thousand

paragraphs.text: "He looked up to heaven": the Lord wants to teach us that in our need we have no help but our heavenly Father.
"Blessed": because He is God, the source of every blessing, and "brake" means that He is responsible for dividing the good things and the blessings among all His creation, and His Church especially.

"Gave them to his disciples": God respects the role of His servants, so He does the work that they cannot do, but they have their role in the labor, and then in rejoicing in the work of God, especially after everyone had eaten and was filled.

entries.section: (4) The return of the twelve and the feeding of the five thousand

paragraphs.text: The crowd was great and the food was plentiful. And St. Matthew adds to St. Mark that: "They that had eaten were about five thousand men, beside women and children" (14:21). And what remained of the fragments was twelve baskets, corresponding to the number of the disciples, so that each one of them might be a witness to this miracle for himself, for St. John mentions (6:12) that it was Christ who charged the disciples with gathering the fragments.
The following is noted:
(1) That this miracle is the only one that the four Gospels mentioned because of the fame it brought to the Lord Christ, for everyone of the crowd who ate became a preacher of it (Mt 14:15-21; Lk 9:

(2) Because of the importance of this miracle, the Church placed it in the readings of her Liturgies, and it is read on the fifth Sunday of the Coptic month, which is usually called "the Sunday of the Blessing."

(3) Among the loveliest spiritual meanings in this miracle is the offering of your few resources in the hand of Christ, even if only a few minutes in the day ... offer them faithfully, and let God bless them and multiply them, so that you are filled first ... and fill others, and then be a witness and servant of His.
(4) The gathering of the fragments teaches us not to be wasteful in the breaking of bread, for often we throw what is left over from us into the rubbish, while others may not find it.

"And straightway": that is, after the filling of the crowds, He commanded His disciples to take the boat and go toward Bethsaida. But He Himself waited to accomplish two things, which were: sending away the crowds with the tenderness of a father bidding farewell to his children. And the second thing was withdrawing by Himself for prayer, in a practical lesson to all servants that the service of the crowds should not draw them away from caring to be alone with God and speak with Him. For there is no work in the life of the faithful servant more splendid than standing and speaking with God, so that he casts all his problems on his Father, and thanks Him for His great works with him.

"When even was come": that is, the time of sunset, for the Jews had two evenings, the first being the time of the afternoon in which the miracle of the feeding took place, and the second the time of sunset. And St. Matthew mentioned both evenings in his account (14:15, 23), and Christ was standing on the shore, looking at the ship in the midst of the sea, which was raging greatly, so that the disciples were afraid and were making every effort at rowing for the saving of their lives.

"The fourth watch": that is, the last part of the night, roughly from three in the morning until the end of the dawn, and this indicates that Christ left them in a very long and hard struggle, and did not intervene except at the last moment. And this means that God may leave us for a time so that we strive against the currents (lusts and difficulties), for striving unto blood (Heb 12:4) is required of us ... for God loves us and He is the shepherd of our souls. But in His wisdom He knows when to leave us and when to hasten to rescue us ... for there is a difference between love and the pampering that spoils a man. "Walking": ... that is, He left the shore and walked on the water to rescue them. And from the darkness and fear, they thought that He had passed by the ship ... and could not make out His features, and thought Him a ghost or a phantom, so their fear increased to the point of crying out. "Would have passed by them": passing by here does not mean "leaving," but He intended to get a little ahead of them so that they might see Him.

The disturbance and fear increased with the psychological exhaustion of the struggle with the sea all night, and here came the words of Christ: "Be of good cheer: it is I; be not afraid." And when He went up into the ship, the wind ceased entirely, which greatly astonished the disciples.
So it is, beloved ... if Christ enters our lives, there is calm and rest and reassurance ... for there is no peace outside Christ, and no peace like the peace of Christ.

"They considered not the miracle of the loaves": that is, the cause of their wonder and fear was their failure to realize that the God who was able to fill the crowds from five loaves is Himself able to walk on the water. "Their heart was hardened": that is, it had not yet been lit with complete faith ... and this happens to us often in times of affliction, for we forget the earlier good works of God.

The ship crossed over to the land of Gennesaret (a plain on the western side of the sea south of Capernaum) and anchored there, and the people recognized Him when He came out of the ship, though it was early morning.

The people began to gather their sick, including the lame among them, to bring them to Christ to obtain healing. And every place Christ entered, He would heal their sick; and to show the large numbers of those who were healed, St. Mark mentions that as many as touched Him were made whole.
The clean and the unclean, the healing of the Canaanite woman's daughter, the healing of the deaf man with an impediment

entries.section: (1) The answer to the scribes and Pharisees and the rebuke of them

paragraphs.text: "Which came from Jerusalem": for the scribes and Pharisees to leave Jerusalem was unusual ... so we are before a delegation that went to Capernaum to investigate the facts about the phenomenon of this man whose fame had spread and who had drawn thousands to himself, whether by his teaching or his miracles. And feelings of jealousy possessed their hearts, more than their desire to see the truth ... and for this reason the first thing that shocked them was that they saw the disciples of Christ eating bread without washing their hands, and for this reason they condemned them for this action.

entries.section: (1) The answer to the scribes and Pharisees and the rebuke of them

paragraphs.text: In these two verses St. Mark gives an important background for the reader of his Gospel, because he was writing for non-Jews about some of the customs of the Pharisees and of the Jews in general, so that the reader might understand why they blamed the disciples in (v. 2), and as an introduction to their conversation with Christ in (v. 5). So he explains to us their concern for outward cleanliness and their counting it as purification, and washing before eating in their houses, or in the case of their buying any produce from the markets, which could not be eaten without washing the hands, and this cleanliness included also all their vessels, and even the beds on which they lay.

entries.section: (1) The answer to the scribes and Pharisees and the rebuke of them

paragraphs.text: The delegation asked the Lord Christ about the reason His disciples violated the religious customs that they had received from their forefathers and fathers.

entries.section: (1) The answer to the scribes and Pharisees and the rebuke of them

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ began His answer by rebuking the scribes and Pharisees, reminding them of what Isaiah prophesied about them (Isa 29:13), making clear their hypocrisy, in that their honoring of God is theoretical, they say something with their tongues and what is inside the heart is something else, so their outward worship becomes without benefit, and likewise their teachings are human teachings springing from their own thoughts and not from the Spirit of God the Holy ... And we also would be hypocrites if we were concerned to show people our religiosity, so as to have a good reputation, without having the true good conduct ... or to bring out our virtues and the sins of others, while we allow our hearts to remain far from God.

entries.section: (1) The answer to the scribes and Pharisees and the rebuke of them

paragraphs.text: Thus outward worship (hypocrisy) leads a person on a road that separates him from the commandment of God and its true purpose; and Satan misleads him with trivial matters, and gives them first importance, so that he spends all his concern on them, and without knowing it, he is thereby rejecting God Himself.

My dear friend ... when God commanded man in the Law to purify himself and wash, this was a reference to purity of heart and thought ... bodily cleanliness is something important, but cleanliness of the heart from jealousy, envy and strife is more important ... so are you careful, before Communion for example, about the purity of your heart and soul, or do you care about the purity of your body? May we examine our thoughts and intentions, and wash them with repentance as we wash our bodies with water.

entries.section: (1) The answer to the scribes and Pharisees and the rebuke of them

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ gives them an example that shows the deviation of their teaching and the corruption of the tradition of their elders ... for while God commanded, in the Law of Moses, the honoring of father and mother (Ex 20:12), and that death should be the punishment for the son who curses either of them, because of the greatness of their standing, likewise in (v. 11), the elders of the Jews came with a strange teaching that contradicts the commandment of God, which is that offering the Corban (gifts) to the temple is more lasting and more binding upon a person than giving it to his needy parents?!! And this tradition is a clear violation of the commandment of honor, and in truth it benefits no one but the elders of the Jews. And so in (v. 12): you prevent people from caring for their parents because of your human teaching, contradicting the command of God. And it is not this teaching only, for there are many other matters by which you have broken the commandment of God, you hypocrites.

Christ wanted His words and teaching to be all-embracing, so He directed His speech to the crowd, after He had been addressing the scribes and Pharisees. And to draw their attention, He said to them: "Hearken unto me every one of you, and understand."
"There is nothing from without": what is meant by it is foods, whether washed or unwashed, and likewise the hands holding this food.
"The things which come out": that is, evil speech, such as condemnation, cursing and lying, and likewise looks of evil lust, for these are what defile the whole man.
"... ears to hear, let him hear": an expression that Christ used often to indicate the importance of what He spoke and taught ... and it may also be said that "two ears" means:
The first ear: the outer ear that hears.
The second ear: the inner will that understands and acts.

And the general meaning intended is: the Lord Christ wanted to move people from the literal understanding of the commandment to the depth of its spiritual meaning, for when God spoke of the unclean animals and the clean animals in the Law of Moses, He intended what lies behind that...
First: to put a separation between what His people eat and what the pagans eat, so that He keeps His people from mixing or from the worship of the Gentiles.
Second: and it is the deeper meaning of this verse, that true purity and uncleanness have their source in the heart and mind of man, and not in what comes to him from outside.

"And when he was entered into the house, his disciples asked him": as usual, when something was hard for the disciples, they would ask Christ about it again away from the crowds, and Christ answered with the same meaning explained in the two preceding verses.

The explanation here is still directed to Christ's disciples, so He makes clear to them that food does not affect the spiritual condition of man (the heart), which is the basic measure before God, for the waste of the food after its digestion goes out of the body, so the body rids itself of what is harmful, and the intestines absorb from it what is useful, and thus the heart is not affected by foods, but remains pure.

The meaning was explained in (vv. 15-16), but the Lord Christ adds here the kinds of sins that come out of the heart and the unclean, evil conscience, such as thoughts of adultery, and thoughts of fornication, that is, licentiousness, murder, theft, covetousness, that is, excessive love of money and of self, and thoughts of wickedness, which means harboring evil toward another, and deceit, which is every kind of trickery, and lasciviousness, meaning the release of all the lusts such as perversion, and the evil eye, which comes in the sense of envy and jealousy or looking at things that stir up base lusts, and blasphemy, and pride, that is, man's self-importance and contempt for others and justifying himself before God, and foolishness. And all these have as their source not food that defiles a man, but an evil heart and mind that defile the whole man, and our allowing the evil thoughts with which Satan speaks to us is a pollution of the heart and mind, so do not open a dialogue with Satan, close the door of discussion with him completely.

How wonderful is the spirituality of the rite of the Liturgy of our Church, when the priest prays secretly in outpouring, saying: "Remember, O Lord, my weakness ... and because of my sins in particular and the uncleanness of my heart, do not withhold from Thy people the grace of Thy Holy Spirit." By this prayer the priest expresses the cry of us all to God that He cleanse our hearts and thoughts and intentions before partaking of His divine Mysteries, and it is a spirit of humility that the rite teaches the priest and all of us, and it confirms what Christ taught, that uncleanness has its source in the heart, and nothing washes it but repentance and the Blood of Christ offered on His holy altar.

The Lord left the region of Capernaum and went to the parts of Tyre and Sidon (two cities 80 kilometers west of Capernaum, lying on the Mediterranean Sea in present-day Lebanon). And Christ's going there was for more than one reason, the most important being:

The first: to get away from the evil and the lying in wait that had become evident from the scribes and Pharisees. The second: His concern for the salvation of the non-Jewish Gentiles ... for Christ's salvation is for all on condition of faith in Him. And although Christ tried not to make Himself known, perhaps to be alone with Himself and His disciples, the news of His arrival had spread.
"The coasts of Tyre and Sidon": the word coasts (borders) means boundaries ... and it comes here in the sense of the lands neighboring Tyre and Sidon.
"Fell at his feet": it makes clear the bad condition of the woman and the severity of her problem, her hope in Christ, and above all her humility.
"A Greek" (a Gentile): this title was applied to non-Jews, and it was a hateful title to them.
"A Syrophenician": that is, present-day Lebanon and the region of the Levant, and the name Syria was mentioned to distinguish her from the (Phoenicians of Libya) in North Africa.

And the meaning is: when Christ reached this region, this woman, a stranger to the people of Christ, came asking Him for healing for her daughter, whom Satan possessed, of course after she had heard from the crowd about the Lord's miracles, and St. Matthew adds (15:23) to what St. Mark mentioned that she was crying out after Him before He entered the house, and that the disciples asked the Lord to heal her and He did not listen to them at first.

The Lord's answer seemed harsh, but by this answer He wanted to make clear the error of the Jews' opinion of the Gentiles, in considering themselves "children" and everyone else "dogs." Likewise the Lord's answer was not lowering the woman's worth in this statement, and He also wanted afterward to make clear the depth of the woman's faith and the extent of her humility. As for her humble reply, and her not objecting or going away, but agreeing to what seemed an insult, it made the Lord bless the steadfastness of her faith and her hope in Him, and respond to her request, and tell her that her daughter was healed and she should go to her ... from which it is clear that His power to crush the demons is very great, for His power surpasses all distances.

So the woman did, and returned to her house to find her daughter completely healed, and that the demon had gone out of her. And the phrase "laid upon the bed" means rest and sleeping in peace, and not the result of the raging that had afflicted her at first ... see also the commentary on the same miracle in Mt 15:22-28.

My dear friend ... do you not agree with me that the woman's humility and the confidence of her faith were behind the answer to her petition? Read with me, beloved, what the Holy Spirit says about the petition of the humble: "The prayer of the humble pierceth the clouds: and till it come nigh, it will not rest; and it will not depart till the most High shall visit, and judge righteously, and execute judgment" (Sir 35:21).
So the humble man is the one whose petition pierces heaven and remains before the throne of God until He answers it ... May we, my God, learn from this woman humility, confidence and importunity.

entries.section: (4) The healing of the deaf man with an impediment in his speech

paragraphs.text: The Lord Jesus' stay in the parts of Tyre and Sidon did not last long, lest the Jews be offended at Him when they saw Him preaching to the Gentiles, so He returned to the east again toward the Sea of Galilee to the Decapolis (spoken of before in ch. 5:20).

entries.section: (4) The healing of the deaf man with an impediment in his speech

paragraphs.text: "And they bring unto him": what is meant of course is the family of the deaf man who had an impediment in his speech, that is, the deaf and dumb, and as is known, one born deaf cannot learn to speak, and so becomes dumb. And the symbolic meaning of this illness is that the man who does not hear the word of God also becomes dumb in the truth and in witnessing to His name. "To put his hand upon him": a reference to their hope of the healing of the sick man by the mere touch of the Lord.

entries.section: (4) The healing of the deaf man with an impediment in his speech

paragraphs.text: The Lord took this sick man aside, out of concern for him, for Christ cares for all His people and His Church. But each one of us has a special place in His heart. So remember, beloved, that when you are alone with Christ in your inner chamber, He is yours and you are His.
What the Lord Jesus did in this miracle:
a) "Put his fingers into his ears": that is, He touched his ears. And of course the deaf and dumb man cannot hear or understand, but he can distinguish the touch that means love and compassion.

b) "He spit, and touched his tongue": that is, He put His finger on his tongue, then took of His spittle and touched the tongue of the dumb man, to show that the power of healing was going forth from Him.

c) "Looking up to heaven": to declare that He and the Father are one, and to teach us that heaven is our help. d) "He sighed": that is, He uttered a deep sound like a groan, by which He expressed His pain and tenderness toward this man before his healing.
e) "And saith unto him": that is, He commanded him by His authority alone.
f) "Ephphatha": that is, "Be opened," and what is meant by that is the ears and the tongue together.

entries.section: (4) The healing of the deaf man with an impediment in his speech

paragraphs.text: Straightway, that is, at once, the healing took place, "and he spake plain," that is, the speech came from his lips sound like that of one accustomed to speech from his childhood, for God always does a perfect work in the life of man. "He charged them that they should tell no man": Christ asked, in His humility and in His flight from the glory of men, which He does not accept, the family of the one who was healed and the crowd not to spread the news of the miracle. But, as much as He charged them, they did the opposite, for "so much the more a great deal they published it," that is, they spread it completely, in a state of amazement, confessing that all the works of Christ were good.
"He maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak": the use of the plural form here indicates that there were other miracles for the deaf and the dumb, but they were not all mentioned...

My beloved God ... loose my tongue with Your praise and thanksgiving in my prayer ... make me speak with You always about everything and all the time ... open my ears to hear and respond to Your repeated calls, for how sweet is the hearing of Your voice, and how good is speaking with You!!
Chapter 8: the feeding of the crowds, the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, the healing of the blind man, the foretelling of death and resurrection

entries.section: (1) The feeding of the crowds with the seven loaves

paragraphs.text: "Dalmanutha": a small, little-known village on the Sea of Galilee, near "Magdala," the town of Mary Magdalene.

entries.section: (2) Christ's warning against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: "And the Pharisees came forth": an expression that St. Mark intended to show that they were like cunning foxes, which had been hiding, and then came out to get at their prey.
"Began to question with him ... tempting him": it also shows us that the purpose of the questioning was not benefit and learning, but the hunting of faults.

"And he sighed deeply in his spirit": that is, the Lord grieved and was sorry over their state and their bad intention, and refused to do a miracle for them, for it was fitting for them to believe in everything He had already done, and to turn to their function of teaching the people instead of tempting Christ.

"He left them ... and departed": the Lord Christ teaches us an important lesson, which is not to waste our time with the many provokers who seek nothing but argument and useless chatter, but consume our energy and effort for nothing ... so beware, beloved, of these.

entries.section: (2) Christ's warning against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: In the haste of their affairs, the disciples forgot to take bread with them, and they had in the ship only one loaf. And St. Mark mentioned this as an introduction to the disciples' misunderstanding of Christ's meaning in (vv. 15-16).

entries.section: (2) Christ's warning against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: In the ship, Christ began to warn the disciples against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees (Mt 12:1) and the leaven of the wicked Herod, and described their hypocrisy as the malignant leaven buried in the dough, whose evil is not apparent, but is spreading. But the disciples understood that Christ was speaking about bread (leaven), so they remembered their forgetting to buy bread for their food.

entries.section: (2) Christ's warning against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: The Lord knew their talk and their limited understanding, so He asked them, in rebuke, seven questions, which He directs to us also after all He has done with us:
Q1: "Why reason ye, because ye have no bread?" What is the reason for the intense thinking about bread, "material things"? (Answer: because we are not yet spiritual.
Q2: "Perceive ye not yet?!" Why do your feelings not move with love toward Me? (Answer: because we love many things ... more than You, O Lord!!
Q3: "Neither understand?" Where are your minds after all My works? (Answer: our minds are full of the thoughts of this world.
Q4: "Have ye your heart yet hardened?" How much time is needed for your hearts to be moved to repentance? (Q5:
its meaning? (Answer: a very long time!!!

"Having eyes, see ye not?" Do you grieve over everything you see? (Answer: no, for often superficiality takes hold of us and we do not understand the depth of Your purposes. "And having ears, hear ye not?" Do you forget My sayings like this? Q6:
and My commandments and My teaching? (Answer: our memory also is superficial, O Lord.
"How many baskets full of fragments ... and how many baskets full of fragments Q7:

took ye up?" Does the repetition of My work with you have its effect in increasing your faith in Me?! (Answer: yes, O Lord, for if we remember we shall believe, and our confidence will increase and we shall be encouraged, and we shall not again fear any apparent lack, for You will make it up for us.

entries.section: (2) Christ's warning against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees

paragraphs.text: "How is it that ye do not understand?": this is the last reproach, with which the Lord sums up all that went before, that our failure to understand always has its basis in man's forgetting the work of God in his life.

Help us then, O my God, not to forget, and visit us always with Your love, and prolong Your longsuffering toward us ... for if we forget, You do not forget us, but continue Your mercies to us as a mother prolongs her patience with her little ones...

entries.section: (3) The healing of the blind man in two stages

paragraphs.text: "Bethsaida": a village at the north of the Sea of Galilee on both banks of the river Jordan, and it is the town of Andrew, Peter and Philip, where they brought to Him a blind man (his relatives), believing, like the faith of the woman with the issue of blood, that Christ would touch and he would be healed.

entries.section: (3) The healing of the blind man in two stages

paragraphs.text: "He took the blind man by the hand": a figure of the fact that Christ takes mankind by the hand so that it does not fall into sin, because: "If the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch" (Mt 15:14).
"Led him out of the town": the town signifies the crowding of the world, so a person must take himself out of his daily occupations so that he can be alone with God and be pained in his works.

As for the direct meaning of leading him out, it is, first: that Christ does not seek fame or glory from men. Second: a reference to the faith and hope of the blind man, which made Christ, though a stranger to him, lead him. "Spit": an act that Christ used more than once in miracles of healing, and the purpose of it is that He gives and grants healing from within Himself, that is, His essence, that is, the authority of His divinity.
"Put his hands upon him": to make him feel secure; and this is the overflow of Christ's constant tenderness toward us ... may we feel that we deserve it!

"He asked him if he saw ought": Christ has no need to ask anyone, for He knows everything, but He did this to teach us that he who asks learns, for how many are the things that God hides from the wise and prudent, and reveals unto babes (Lk 10:21).

entries.section: (3) The healing of the blind man in two stages

paragraphs.text: When Christ asked him about his ability to see, he answered that he now saw partially, men as trees. And this healing in stages is a reference to gradual growth in the spiritual life, and the repentance after which man sees things clearly.

And this teaches us, if we are servants, to be gentle with the penitents returning to the bosom of the Church, for perhaps all the truths of the faith are not yet clear to them, but they are beloved to the heart of God, and they may precede us into the Kingdom.

entries.section: (3) The healing of the blind man in two stages

paragraphs.text: Christ then touched his eyes to complete his healing ... as if saying to us all, and to everyone who has begun the journey of spiritual healing: My hand is with you to support you and to complete your healing, and to give you complete spiritual insight so that you can discern all things.
And as was Christ's custom, He commanded him not to tell anyone of this miracle, to confirm His flight from the praise of men ... and to teach us to hide the good deeds that God has given us to do.

"Caesarea Philippi": a city in northern Galilee where there was pagan worship of one of the gods of the Greeks, and its present name is "Banias." In the time of Christ, Philip the son of Herod the Great rebuilt it, and named it "Caesarea" as a courtesy to Caesar of Rome, so it bore his name and became "Caesarea Philippi."

On the way from Galilee to the region of Caesarea Philippi, He asked His disciples, saying to them: "Whom do men say that I am?" And their answer differed according to what each of them had heard, for some people claimed that He was John whom God raised after his killing (and this was the opinion of Herod himself), and others said He was Elijah who precedes the Christ according to the prophecy of Malachi: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the day of the LORD" (Mal 4:5), and the saying of St. Mark here agrees with what St. Matthew mentioned (16:14) that others said He was Jeremiah or one of the prophets risen from the dead.

Christ asked the disciples a second question completing His previous question, which was: But whom say ye that I am? And Peter answered that He is the Christ Himself, the hope of the whole world. And St. Matthew added (16:17) to what St. Mark mentioned here two things: a) Christ's praise of Peter that he uttered this truth of the faith. b) the declaration that it was not possible for Peter to know this truth except by a revelation from heaven (the Holy Spirit) to him; see the commentary on (Mt 16:16-17). But Christ charged His disciples that they should tell no man of this secret, for His hour had not yet come, and the time for declaring His glory after His crucifixion had not yet come.

My beloved brother ... the situation of the Jews' giving their opinion of the person of Christ, that He was Elijah or Jeremiah or another prophet, reminds us of the situation of many of us in these days, for a person sees God as he wants God to be, and not God in His complete reality ... for some see God as merciful without justice, and others see Him as a harsh judge without mercy ... but our Church teaches us, by spiritual balance, to see God through all His attributes and commandments, for He is the merciful and the just, the good and the decisive together, and how dangerous it is to rely on one attribute or one verse that describes God.

entries.section: (5) The foretelling of death and resurrection

paragraphs.text: After Peter and the disciples acknowledged that Jesus is the awaited Christ and the hope of the Gentiles, Christ began to tell them what was to be expected of the plotting of the leaders of the Jews and their priests and His being handed over, and that He would go through many sufferings, beginning with His trial until His crucifixion and death, and then His resurrection on the third day. But these words did not please Peter, who took Christ aside, and began to rebuke Him strongly for what He had said. And at this time Peter did not care about what Christ desired, but on the contrary, rushed after his natural human feelings, and did not see in Christ the suffering Servant of whom Isaiah prophesied (Isa 53:2-3), for the Christian life often means hard work and deprivation and deep suffering ... so fix your gaze on the resurrection that follows the Cross.

entries.section: (5) The foretelling of death and resurrection

paragraphs.text: "But when he had turned about and looked on his disciples": before Christ directed His rebuke to Peter, He looked at His disciples so that His words might be directed to everyone who shared Peter's limited thinking. As for the severe rebuke of Peter, it came as a result of the limitation of his understanding of Christ's redemption of the world, for his concern was confined to the earthly kingship of Christ, and that is the concern of most people, and not the concern of God for the salvation of men.
"Satan": despite the difficulty of the word, Christ intended by it to affirm that there is no one who wants to hinder the redemption except Satan himself.

entries.section: (5) The foretelling of death and resurrection

paragraphs.text: The speech here is directed to the disciples, and the Church, and all believers after them. Whoever wants to follow Christ must accept the idea of bearing the cross, and the acceptance of suffering from persecution and leaving family and friends and other things, and no one can do this unless he denies himself (his own self), and humbles himself in true love before his Lord, who went through suffering first.

And Christ affirms that the salvation of the soul requires of it striving and leaving material luxury and its selfishness and its lusts, which are obstacles to its salvation, and that it set out in service and preaching, and this will be the way of its deliverance ... for nothing compares with what it will gain with Christ.

entries.section: (5) The foretelling of death and resurrection

paragraphs.text: Christ is still directing His speech to us all, and warns us that all the material gains of the world we shall find hollow and empty, not equal to the loss of the soul and its destruction, and that all the wealth of the world, if a man offered it, would not redeem his soul, whose price is the Blood of Christ alone ... for by following Christ we know the meaning of true life while we are on earth, and we shall have eternal life also...

entries.section: (5) The foretelling of death and resurrection

paragraphs.text: Everyone who neglects Christ's words here, or is ashamed of His sufferings and His Cross, will have no place or share in His Kingdom at His Second Coming...

My beloved Lord ... in many cases I find myself refusing suffering and persecution and the way of the Cross, and I do not know that in this way I refuse You, and lose my portion with You ... teach me, my Lord, and reveal to my eyes and heart the lowliness of this world and all its material things, so that I set out toward You, caring for nothing but to follow Your steps, imitating You, so as to please Your heart first, and win my crown in Your Kingdom ... Amen. (ch. 9:1):
And He said unto them: "Verily I say unto you, That there be some of them that stand here, which shall not taste of death, till they have seen the kingdom of God come with power."

"Them that stand here": that is, some of the disciples will not die before they see the signs of the beginning of the Kingdom of God and its spread with power, by the spread of the preaching and the Gentiles' acceptance of the faith, and the clear marks of the Church, for the Kingdom of God means that God reigns over the hearts of the people who believe in His name...
The Transfiguration, the healing of a demoniac, a conversation with the disciples

About a week after Christ's earlier talk about His sufferings, His death and His resurrection, and about His Kingdom coming with power, He took with Him three of His disciples, who enjoyed more love and faith than the others, and went up with them onto a high mountain. There His appearance (form) was changed before them, and He appeared in great glory, as we shall see. But the following meanings concern us here:

(1) Only three disciples: with God there is no partiality, but the one who is better prepared receives greater blessings. (2) A high mountain: no one can behold the glories of God unless he rises up and the world grows small before his eyes.

St. Mark here describes the manner of this change in the Lord's appearance, for His garments became exceedingly white, shining like light or radiance. To show the intensity of the brightness, he added that no fuller on earth can whiten them so. The fuller is the one who whitens cloth, as the last step in the making of spun and woven fabric.

And together with the change of His appearance into this glory, Elijah appeared to them, who represents the prophets and the living (because he had not yet died), and represents virginity and its high degree (because he did not marry). Moses also appeared, who represents those who have fallen asleep in the hope of Christ's redemption, and also the spiritual leadership of the people of God. Both of them fasted forty days, as a symbol of the holiness in which they lived on earth, and also as a symbol of the form of the spiritual life, whether in monasticism or in the sacrament of marriage. And in honor of them, St. Mark added that they were talking with Jesus.
My beloved brother ... have we thought about obtaining the honor and blessings of talking with Jesus?!!

With the surprise, awesomeness and splendor of the sight, Peter spoke, declaring his happiness with this vision, and that heavenly spiritual feelings are better than earthly emotions however splendid they may be. But he also added, according to his human thinking, that Christ with Elijah and Moses might be in need of tabernacles to shelter them. St. Mark attributes this saying of Peter to the state of terror he was in during the transfiguration.

"A cloud that overshadowed them": St. Matthew added (Mt 17:5) that this cloud was "bright", to indicate the divine presence, just as the bright cloud appeared to Aaron (Ex 16:10) ... And the appearance of the cloud was accompanied by the Father's declaration concerning His Son and His divinity, exactly as happened at the Baptism of Christ.

And suddenly the heavenly scene ended, and the form of the Lord returned to its first nature, and Moses and Elijah disappeared. And as they came down, Christ charged them to tell no one what they had seen until after He had risen from the dead. Yet they did not understand at that time the meaning of His rising from the dead, but they did not ask Him about it; rather they kept everything to themselves (within them).
Comment on the transfiguration:
(1) Perhaps the disciples recognized the persons of Moses and Elijah either by the Spirit, or because Christ pronounced their names during the conversation.

2) "(It is good for us to be here": a life of contemplation and retreat is good for the servant and the spiritual person, for he takes from it provision and strength that help him to go down to the field of service and suffering.

(3) Christ's conversation with Elijah and Moses shows that there is unceasing speech between God and His saints. Therefore the Church teaches us that, besides speaking with God, we can speak with the saints in our prayers (without worshiping them).

(4) If the sight was so splendid to this degree, how will the sight be in heaven, my friend?! Come ... take courage ... how beautiful is heaven with its Christ and its saints!! And do not forget that you have a place there.

The appearance of Elijah at the transfiguration raised a question among the disciples, which they put to Christ: the scribes teach the people that Elijah must appear first, before the appearance of Christ; and if what we have seen is what is meant, how can Elijah's appearance be after Christ?!
"Elijah indeed comes first": that is, what the scribes say is correct in this teaching, that Elijah precedes the appearance of Christ.
"And restores all things": that is, he brings the Jews back by repentance, in preparation for receiving Christ.
"That He must suffer many things and be set at nought": the disciples had a limited outlook, and so they did not understand that Christ must suffer (Isa; 53:2, Ps 22:6).

"Elijah ... is come": a clear reference to John the Baptist, who resembled Elijah in his work and in his person. John came and the Jews killed him (they did to him whatever they wished). See also the explanation of (Mt 17:10-13).

entries.section: (3) The healing of a boy with an unclean spirit

paragraphs.text: "Greatly amazed, and running": St. Mark depicts the state of the crowd on seeing Christ, for they ran to Him out of their joy ... As for their amazement, it was because of His sudden absence and their not knowing where He was. After the transfiguration, the Lord Jesus returned with His three disciples to the rest of the disciples, and found many questioning them, among them the scribes, who seized the opportunity of the Teacher's absence to embarrass the disciples. Therefore, when Christ arrived, the first thing He said was a question to the scribes: "What question ye with them?" The purpose of His question was to relieve His disciples of the embarrassment and to answer on their behalf.

entries.section: (3) The healing of a boy with an unclean spirit

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ received no answer from the scribes, for a man in great need interrupted the conversation, saying: I have brought unto Thee my son, which hath a dumb spirit, and I did not find You. And St. Luke adds that he was his father's only child (Lk 9:38). St. Mark mentioned this story here to show that our struggle with Satan continues, and that faith in Christ is necessary for victory over him to be achieved ... And the man began to explain the symptoms of Satan's dwelling in him and raging.
"Wheresoever he taketh him": when Satan rages against him.
"He teareth him": he subjects him to severe fits, so that he makes involuntary movements by which he harms himself.

"And he foameth, and gnasheth with his teeth": symptoms resembling epilepsy, so that the mouth convulses and the saliva flows, and all his muscles stiffen and he loses the ability to move ... "And I spake to thy disciples" - in Your absence - "that they should cast him out; and they could not."

entries.section: (3) The healing of a boy with an unclean spirit

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ answered with a reply that carried a rebuke. But for whom was this rebuke?
"O faithless generation":
First: the rebuke may be for the disciples, who, because of the weakness of their faith, were not able to cast out this devil and heal the sufferer.
Second: perhaps the blame is for the father who - despite his need - was doubtful, and his faith was not complete, for he said in his words to Christ: "If Thou canst do any thing?"
Third: the blame may be for the whole crowd, which had seen so many earlier miracles and did not believe, as shown by the Lord's saying: "O generation".

"How long shall I suffer you?": Of course Christ bore much, and will also bear, the weaknesses of His disciples, especially at His passion and crucifixion ... But what is meant here is to make clear that God's heart cannot bear unbelief in Him or doubt of Him, for this wounds Him greatly. Therefore He also rebuked the disciples for their little faith ... and in the incident of the sea raging against the boat (Mt 8:23-26), and also when He rebuked Peter when he doubted and began to sink (Mt 14:25-32).
"Bring him unto Me": proof of the Lord Jesus' tenderness toward us, and a confirmation of His saying in (Mt 11:28): "Come unto Me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

entries.section: (3) The healing of a boy with an unclean spirit

paragraphs.text: When the boy came near to Christ, Satan raged exceedingly, so that he cast the boy down cruelly, and he wallowed and foamed (his saliva flowed).
... This teaches us Satan's cruelty and evil on the one hand, and also shows that he knew he was certainly going out. Therefore it is as though he were fighting in despair his last war...

entries.section: (3) The healing of a boy with an unclean spirit

paragraphs.text: "How long is it ago?": Of course Christ knew everything, but the purpose of the question is to make clear to the crowd, and teach them, that nothing is difficult for Him however long the time, or however long the cruelty and severity of the sickness.
And the father went on in his answer, explaining other things Satan had done to his son, for he tried to kill him many times, and often cast him into the fire and into the water to destroy him.

"If Thou canst": a question that reflects the man's hope that Christ was able to heal his son on the one hand, and in its tone also carries doubt of this ability on the other hand, or let us say weakness of faith. "Have compassion on us, and help us": that is, the son and the father, and on his mother and all his family.

entries.section: (3) The healing of a boy with an unclean spirit

paragraphs.text: "If Thou canst": Christ answered the man with the same words as he had asked, and the meaning is: I can do all things, but My work, and all My works, are seen only by the one who believes in this power of Mine; and your doubt and the weakness of your faith is the greatest obstacle to your son's healing.

entries.section: (3) The healing of a boy with an unclean spirit

paragraphs.text: "Cried out ... with tears": the man's answer came expressing his state. His crying out meant: I have no hope but You. And his tears express his weakness and his apology for his lack of trust. Then he declared his faith, and expressed that he was truly weak in faith, asking Christ's help in strengthening and completing his incomplete faith.

entries.section: (3) The healing of a boy with an unclean spirit

paragraphs.text: The crowd grew exceedingly, and Christ commanded Satan to come out by rebuking him, describing him as unclean - like all his kingdom - and called him: "Thou dumb and deaf spirit", to make clear that Satan is the cause of these two symptoms.

"I charge thee": this shows us the divinity of Christ and His absolute authority over the kingdom of darkness and its powers, and that none of it can resist Him or disobey Him. So He went on: "come out of him, and enter no more into him", that is, do not return to him again.

entries.section: (3) The healing of a boy with an unclean spirit

paragraphs.text: "And cried": the defeated and despairing Satan is the one crying out here, expressing his fury at coming out, and so he threw the boy to the ground, fainting and motionless, until many thought that he was dead. But Christ, in His tenderness, went up to the boy and took him by the hand ... and raised him, and he rose up with Him, healed of every sickness.

entries.section: (3) The healing of a boy with an unclean spirit

paragraphs.text: After the end of the event, when the disciples were alone with Christ, they asked Him the secret of their inability, and whether they had lost their authority over unclean spirits given to them in (Mt 10:1), or what? Christ's answer to them came: the gift given by God must be preserved by the spiritual life, represented in asking God's constant help "prayer", and in rising above the world and its desires and material things "fasting". So it is, my friend ... we see that faith is the essence of the relationship with God, and without it we lose the sight of His work in our lives. And sadly, currents of rationalism and doubt in God's ability to solve our problems have increased, and worry and anxiety have grown, while the problems remained as they were...

Do you not agree with me that both of us need to cry out in our prayer, saying: "Lord, I believe; help Thou mine unbelief"? And before we begin with our minds, is it not better to experience God's hand in helping us?

entries.section: (4) The announcement of His death and a talk about greatness

paragraphs.text: As the Lord Christ did in the previous chapter (vv. 31-32), (and spoke of His being delivered up, His death and His resurrection, He repeats the same words here in preparing His disciples for the difficult events of the future.

entries.section: (4) The announcement of His death and a talk about greatness

paragraphs.text: "They understood not": not because of the difficulty of the saying itself, for the words are understandable linguistically, but because what the Lord Christ was saying was far from the picture in their imagination of His awaited kingdom with its earthly glory. "And were afraid": that is, they preferred not to ask Him, because of their embarrassment to speak about this matter ... and the truth is that not one of them understood any of Christ's declarations until after the redemption and the resurrection.

entries.section: (4) The announcement of His death and a talk about greatness

paragraphs.text: A conversation went on among the disciples as they walked. And when they arrived at the house (most likely Peter's house), the Lord Christ asked them what had been said among them. The purpose of His question was not to know - for He knows all things - but to teach the disciples and correct a mistaken notion in them, for they were occupied with the thought of who was the greatest among them, and its basis was pride of heart.

entries.section: (4) The announcement of His death and a talk about greatness

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ sat down and gathered His disciples around Him, and began to teach at once: whoever wishes to be greater and lord of all must be a servant, putting himself last of all and less than everyone.

And what Christ teaches here completely contradicts the world's notion of greatness, for the world's greatness is domination, pride and control "... the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them" (Mt 20:25). But the greatness of Christianity is humility, denial of self and service of the other) ... see the explanation of Mt 20:20-28).

entries.section: (4) The announcement of His death and a talk about greatness

paragraphs.text: In tenderness, the Lord Christ took a child and embraced him, while still directing His words to His disciples, saying: whoever offers a work, however small - such as showing tenderness to a child in the name of Christ - Christ considers it a work offered to Himself personally and to the Father who sent Him; what matters is service and self-giving for the sake of others, and not the outward appearance of leadership or greatness.

entries.section: (5) Service in the name of Christ

paragraphs.text: In (v. 37), the Lord said: "Whosoever shall receive ... in My name". Perhaps this saying made John remember an event he had gone through with the disciples, when they saw a man using the Lord's name to cast out devils, and he was not one of the Twelve nor one of the seventy apostles, so zeal seized them and they forbade him because he was not one of them.

entries.section: (5) Service in the name of Christ

paragraphs.text: The Lord reproved them for forbidding him, for the man was a believer and a lover of Christ, and his faith was the reason Satan went out ... whoever has experienced Me and experienced the power of My work with him will not turn against Me or blaspheme My name ... And as long as a man does not resist the truth and the sound faith delivered to the Church by Christ, there is no need to forbid him, otherwise it would become a desire to monopolize gifts and service.

entries.section: (5) Service in the name of Christ

paragraphs.text: So if the deed is small, even if someone gives you - in My name - a cup of water, he shall not lose his reward, how much more then the one who uses My name to have mercy on a sick person and cast a devil out of him?!
Comment:
The Lord says in (v. 40): "He that is not against us is on our part", and in (Mt; 12:30, Lk 11:23):

"He that is not with Me is against Me". At first glance it may seem that the two meanings contradict each other, but in truth the meaning is one, because neutrality in the matter of faith in Christ is impossible; one is either with Him or against Him, with the actions that follow from that. To clarify we say:

The sign of friendship may be not resisting Christ, and so we understand: "He that is not against us - does not resist us - is on our part". And the sign of enmity may be not taking part in the positive work, so we understand: "He that is not with Me - in My work - is against Me".

The teaching here about not causing stumbling is a teaching for the disciples in general, for servants and for all believers, and it shows the seriousness of causing the simple in faith to stumble. And "he who causes to stumble" means the one who was a direct cause of another's error, or caused him confusion and doubts by unsound teaching, a wrong saying or a shameful act.

And because of the seriousness of this sin and its evil in God's sight, He says: it is better for a man that a millstone (a large stone for grinding grain) be hanged about his neck and he be cast into the sea, to die, than that he cause one who is simple in his faith to stumble.
The detailed explanation of this text was given before in (Mt 5:29-30, 18:8-9), and we shall be content here to clarify the following meanings:

"Cut it off ... pluck it out": cutting off the hand or the foot or plucking out the eye is not a literal meaning but a figurative meaning, intended that a man cut off all causes and ways of evil whose source is his senses or the people around him. The Lord Christ used the words "cutting off and plucking out" to show us the degree of decisiveness required of us all in facing stumbling blocks and their entrances, for a small stumbling block produces great evil.

"Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched": another expression that terrifies the one who makes light of God's just recompense, and everyone who is careless about his senses and makes himself stumble, or becomes a cause of stumbling for others ... for the words "dieth not - is not quenched" are evidence of the eternity of the torment and that it does not cease.

So it is, my friend ... all who are deceived by the pleasures of the world and its temporal, passing desires drive themselves to a torment severe in its intensity, and the worse is that it never ends.

The talk in the preceding verses is about fleeing from sin and stumbling, and this is what the Fathers call negative striving. But the talk in this verse is about positive striving, and the intended meaning is: just as every sacrifice offered to God is salted with salt in order to preserve it, so the spiritual person must preserve himself, not only by fleeing and avoiding stumbling blocks, but also by growing in the virtues that preserve him and give him a savor before God, and these virtues are like fire in its light and in spreading warmth to others (Ex 43:24).
Take care, friend, of repentance and constant striving against all sources of stumbling, and flee for your life with all your strength, drawing others with you as far as possible...

But if virtue in the believer's life becomes without saltness, that is, without taste, and faded in color, then the man cannot be accepted by God. Therefore strive to live by virtue so that you may have salt in yourselves, that is, that each of you may have peace with himself, and all of you peace toward one another.

Beloved, give attention in the sacrament of repentance and confession, not only to recounting the obvious sins by which you grieved God's heart, but also declare your shortcoming in the Christian virtues, and ask your father for guidance and training, so that we may all be salted with a salt by which we please our Christ...
Hindrances to reaching God: divorce, love of money, leadership

"And He arose from thence, and cometh": that is, He left Capernaum and headed south to Judea after crossing the river Jordan. And as was the Lord Christ's custom, He began to teach and preach to all who gathered around Him.

"And the Pharisees came ... tempting Him": this also shows us that the Pharisees were following Him, not in order to benefit, but in order to test Him and catch Him in mistakes. Therefore they chose a subject that represents a social controversy, despite the clarity of the commandment about it, namely the subject of divorce.

In the wisdom of Christ and its perfection, He answered their question with a question, namely: what is the commandment that God gave to Moses? They answered with the confidence of teachers that the Law permitted divorce, on condition that a document be written for it, so that by it the woman might marry again if she wished (and it was the custom that the man would first go to one of the wise men to absorb his anger before the bill of divorce was written).

The Lord Christ makes clear what God's purpose was in marriage, and why there was the exception and the permission of divorce. For God, in His plan and purpose, created one man and one woman, that each might belong to the other. But because of the people's turning away from God, the decline of their spiritual level, and their comparison with the pagan peoples who permit adultery and polygamy, God permitted them divorce, but not out of the pleasure of His heart, but perhaps to protect the wife from being killed, or the man from turning to idolatry.

To confirm His answer, the Lord Christ used the same words that Adam uttered in (Gen 2:24) after the creation of Eve - words which the Pharisees know well - and the meaning of these words is as follows:
"For this cause": that is, for the completion of the sacrament of marriage.

"Shall a man leave": that is, the man must become independent of his father's house in order to build his new family. And this independence or leaving does not mean neglecting our duties toward our parents in caring for them, for marital love does not conflict with the commandment to honor parents.
"One flesh": it points to the splendor of the Christian marital union, for by the descent of the Holy Spirit in the prayer of the crowning, the two become one on the level of soul, body and spirit.

After the Lord Christ had made clear the picture of the wonderful marital union in (v. 8), He also makes clear that God is the founder of this union and the One who joins it together, and He is the One who works with the married couple, and in them, so that they may become one flesh. Consequently, man cannot annul a bond or covenant that God established and witnessed. But the Christian must strive together with the work of God's grace in the sacrament of marriage, and struggle in controlling himself, offering love, and bearing the shortcomings and weaknesses of the other however hard this may be. For Christian marriage is not for the pleasing of the self and its desires, but is a call to the breaking of self and selfishness and to submission to the other, as the Church charges us in the prayer of the crowning: "Let each of you submit to the other." Only then does man's will meet God's good will.

As happened often, and in private, the disciples asked the Lord Christ for a further explanation of this dialogue, and He added that the real motive for seeking divorce is that the feelings or desires of the man and the woman are moved toward another party, so he seeks to fulfill his desire by divorcing the first in order to be joined to the second. Therefore God considered divorcing in order to marry to be nothing but the sin of adultery before Him, even if society approves of this second marriage.

My beloved brother ... have you understood now why our Church does not permit divorce except for the cause of adultery? For the Church is entrusted with Christ's commandment, and the pressure of society on her does not move her. And instead of resorting to the easy solutions of divorce, we must establish sound spiritual concepts, and prepare generations and youth to understand the meaning of Christian marriage.

"And they brought": what is meant, of course, is the fathers and mothers of the children, for they felt the holiness of Christ and His blessing. Therefore each of them hurried to bring his children to obtain the blessing by Christ's touching them. And we may infer that this situation caused a crowding and commotion that made the disciples rebuke these parents.

"Much displeased": let it never be understood from this expression as the nervous human emotion into which we may fall in our weakness. But when Christ saw how the disciples had shocked the children's parents with coldness, He said to them: "Suffer the little children to come unto Me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." That is, these children, by their simplicity and purity - which we adults may have lost - have come to own the Kingdom before us.

"Verily I say unto you": it is the expression Christ always used before declaring an important spiritual truth, and here it is: that childhood is a meaning and not an age, so none will enter the Kingdom of God except he who enjoys the virtues of little children, such as innocence, simplicity and trust, which are marks that distinguish the pure children of God, and which the evil world does not know. For God wants from us simplicity, spontaneity and the trust of faith in prayer and in speaking with Him; likewise He wants our dealings with others to be free of craftiness and of the world's satanic wisdom, but to be frank and simple, and not lacking the wisdom of the Holy Spirit ... And after this teaching, the Lord embraced the children with His great tenderness, and granted them His divine blessing.

My beloved God ... I long for my childhood in You ... would that I were one of those children, touching Your knees with my hand, and You touching the locks of my hair with Your hand, so that the current of Your holiness would run through my whole being...
My God ... I know that You have given me much, but I cannot hold back the longing of my heart to throw myself into Your tender embrace!

As the Lord Christ was going out on His way to Jerusalem, a man came and worshiped Him, asking Him about the way to eternal life. And the word "ran" shows that his coming to Christ was out of eagerness and a real motive for knowledge ... and the word "knelt" points to his respect and veneration for Christ.

Sadly, the enemies of Christianity, throughout the ages, have exploited this verse to deny divinity to Christ. To these we say that Christ declared His divinity clearly, as it is in (Jn 10:30): "I and My Father are one."

And to explain what Christ said, we must briefly become acquainted with a Jewish background of this time ... for the priests and the Pharisees forbade the people to use the name of God in conversation, and to be content with mentioning His titles, so they would say the Blessed ... the Most High ... the Good ... and so on.
Therefore, when this man addressed Christ in the previous verse, saying: "Good Master", Christ stopped him in this verse, saying: "Why callest thou Me good?" Is it because you:
realize that I am God, and so ascribe to Me the absolute goodness which belongs to God alone?
speak to Me as people are accustomed, in courtesy toward those they respect, by applying attributes and titles to them?

Christ was not waiting for an answer from the man, but answered his question that the way to the Kingdom is keeping God's commandments and doing them, and the Lord Christ mentioned some of the Ten Commandments; but this answer did not satisfy the one who asked, and he answered in turn that he had known these commandments from childhood.

"Then Jesus beholding him loved him": when Christ saw in this man the eagerness of his question, his humility in his worship, his real concern to keep the commandments from his youth, his attempt to apply them faithfully and sincerely, and his desire to inherit eternal life, He looked at him with a look of love and encouragement before presenting the cure to him and putting His finger on the real sickness of this rich man, which was love of money. Therefore the cure was the complete uprooting of the sin, that he give up his money to the poor, and it would become for him a treasure and a crown in the Kingdom of God. And despite the difficulty of the cure, the Lord Christ did not lighten any of it, but added to it that he follow Him, giving up indulgence and luxury, bearing the cross of self-denial and the acceptance of suffering ... Therefore the man was sad, for he felt the dominion of money over him; and instead of following Christ, he went away grieved!!

My God and my Lord ... I feel in my depths that I have not yet been freed from the love of money, indeed I am this very man ... for I fear and am troubled if anything is lost to me ... You are pointing to my sickness and not his, so will You give me healing?! I beg You, free me from this love that veils You from me, and satisfy me with You, so that all I possess becomes cheap under Your feet, and Your cross becomes the desire of my heart...

In follow-up and comment on the dialogue with the rich man, the Lord Christ spoke of the difficulty of the entrance of those who have riches into the Kingdom of God. And when He noticed the disciples' bewilderment and confusion, He made it clearer to them that money in itself is not a sin, but love of money, reliance on it, boasting in it and hoarding it makes a man depend on it more than on God, and even hardens his heart toward those around him, and the pride of wealth enters him, and he forgets his humility, his need and his thanksgiving to God. And to make clear the difficulty of the salvation of those who rely on their money, Christ gave them a pictorial example, that the passing of a camel - with all its size - through the eye of a needle is easier than the entrance of these into the Kingdom of Heaven, that is, the impossibility of the salvation of everyone who has put money in his hope...

My beloved brother ... do not forget that there were righteous rich men, such as Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, and the Lord did not ask them to leave their money. The sin, then, that dwells in our depths in the midst of this material world, is the love of money itself, and it prevents us from seeing the work of God, so let us repent of it. And instead of wishing for wealth, let us wish for what is more lasting and useful, where no thief comes near and no moth destroys, and that is the Kingdom prepared for us by our rich Father.

When the disciples saw the difficulty of what Christ was teaching, they expressed what was inside them about the difficulty of salvation, saying one to another: "Who then can be saved?" Christ's answer came reassuring: what man cannot do in his striving, God completes by His grace. But we must be faithful in presenting our weaknesses to Him and our longing for the Kingdom, and He is able to complete His salvation in us, for with God all things are possible.

Spontaneously, and as usual, Peter was the quickest of those who spoke with Christ. And perhaps the awesomeness of Christ's last talk is what moved him to seek reassurance for himself and the disciples, who had left all to follow Christ.

"An hundredfold": Christ's answer came explaining and confirming the goodness of God, the maker of good things ... can God be indebted to a man?! For everyone who has left anything for the sake of God and service shall have a hundredfold, and the expression here is figurative, a way of saying the abundance of God's giving to whoever has left and followed Him, so He gives him here spiritual brothers and children, and peace of heart and a rest the world does not know, and He does not leave them in need of any of the necessities of the present material world either, although the matter is not free of persecution and afflictions in this time. But the lasting and permanent compensation is the inheritance of eternal life prepared by God Himself, and they will have a special and distinguished standing, and be nearer to God their Savior and more satisfied with Him...

My beloved brother ... is not this promise of Christ encouraging to us all to give up some of our comfort, our time and our money, in order to go on with Him in following and in true heartfelt spiritual service ... do you not long with me for the taste of the hundredfold?! Come then, come to the Church, and offer even a little of your time for service, for Christ needs all energies for His Church.

The Lord ended His words here with a warning, for the promise of the Kingdom to whoever has left does not create carelessness about the assurance of salvation, but we must be on guard, and complete our striving to the end. Was not Judas among those who left and followed Christ? Yet he turned back and fell away, and loved money and so betrayed Christ! For slackness and carelessness make the one who came later get ahead of the one who was first.

The disciples were like the rest of the Jews, for they understood all of Christ's talks about the Kingdom of Heaven and the Kingdom of God with a material, earthly and limited temporal picture, and the idea of positions and offices occupied some of them. Therefore this dialogue and the request of James and John to sit in the foremost place, that is, on the right and on the left of Christ.

"We desire": the verb came in the past tense to indicate either that the two disciples had already made the same request before, or a reference to the fact that their mother had already made the same request.

"Ye know not": Christ's answer came to make clear the difference between God's plan in the salvation of man, passing through the cross and its sufferings, and man's limited thinking, tied to earthly things and their passing glories. And the Lord completed His talk with a question to the two disciples, whose meaning is: are you able to bear My sufferings on the cross, and to drink the cup of injustice and humiliation to its end?!

"And they said unto Him, We can": without awareness, the answer came quickly and without understanding of Christ's purpose. Therefore Christ answered them with what they would understand later, namely that fellowship in suffering and death would indeed be granted to them, but sitting on His right hand and on His left is for the one who loves God, and strives with more labor and struggle; for God in His justice shows no partiality, and gives each one "according to his own labour" (1 Cor 3:8).

These human feelings, and not spiritual ones, were still master of the situation, for indignation filled the rest of the disciples. And when Christ noticed this, He began to correct their mistakes, explaining to them the concepts of true greatness in His kingdom, and that the greatness of the world is lordship, controlling others and exercising authority over them.

But what I ask of you is true humility. For whoever gives himself and his honor in the service of others becomes great before God. And whoever wants a high standing in the Kingdom must give up his pride, as though he were a slave with no rights. And remember this always, that you follow My example in My Incarnation, for I came giving up My glory, and I sought honor from no one, but served all in true self-giving unto death.

My beloved God ... what You truly did during Your Incarnation was beyond the imagination and understanding even of the angels, but this is Your infinite love and humility ... my God, make me ashamed of my self, which is still seeking its standing and its worldly glory ... make me always lift my eyes toward Your cross, so that it may be my example, that I may set out to serve those around me, giving myself as You did ... Amen.

Passing through Jericho on the way to Jerusalem, blind Bartimaeus heard of Christ's passing, and his cry "Jesus, Thou Son of David, have mercy on me" declared a faith that surpassed many ... for the title "Son of David" is the title of the Messiah the Savior, so he declared and believed in the One whom the priests and Pharisees had rejected. And his hope of healing at His hands is faith in the power of this Savior over all things.
When he cried out for mercy, many rebuked him...

Does not Satan do this with us, trying to silence us from repentance and from asking for mercy? Would that we did as he did and increased our crying out toward God, so that we may win His mercies and His healing for our souls.

"And Jesus stood still": and how could He not stand?! He who is overcome by His tenderness and His love for mankind, and He called the crying one in need. So the blind man cast away his garment - the garment symbolizes man's laziness - and came to Jesus, the fountain of our healing.
Despite the clarity and expectedness of the blind man's request, Christ asked him: "What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?"

And this reminds us of the sick man at Bethesda whom Christ asked: "Wilt thou be made whole?" (Jn 5:6). So Christ wants to teach us something important, namely that man must always declare his will and his insistence before God, whatever his weakness, and Christ is able to cure this weakness or helplessness ... Therefore this man received his healing because of his faith and his insistence ... and he followed Jesus in the way, that is, in His entry into Jerusalem.
