paragraphs.text: Thus the Lord accepted in Himself the sentence of death by His own will and authority before the Jews carried it out on Him, and declared that He would not repeat this mystery with them again on earth, since He was content with instituting it before His death. But He promised that there would be a new feast and fellowship in the Kingdom of Heaven, where we shall be spirits feeling and being satisfied with Him in a spiritual manner far from material eating, and therefore the expression "drink it new" is a figurative expression whose purpose is what has been explained before.

V.: "And when they had sung an hymn": the psalms of praise (Ps 115-118), known to the Jews, were sung after the Passover supper. And when they finished the singing, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

In His last talk with His disciples, and before delivering Himself up, the Lord began to prepare them for the battles they were about to face, and He showed them the first of them, which is doubt of Him, as they would see Him delivered into the hands of the Jews without resistance, and in an appearance of weakness. And as a result of this situation, they would flee and be scattered like sheep that have lost their shepherd, and the Lord here used the same meaning that Zechariah uttered in (Zech 13:7).

The Lord did not leave them long in this state - of anxiety and disturbance - but declared with assurance that He would rise from the dead, and would meet them in Galilee. And of course, not all Christ's words were understood by them, but they came to be sure of them after they happened.

As was Peter's custom, being always the first to speak or object, and with a mistaken feeling about himself that he was better than the rest of the disciples, he declared, with an impulsive, unconsidered emotion, that he was the only one who would not doubt and would not leave Christ, even if he remained alone and the rest of the disciples left Him.

In response to Peter's pride and conceit, Christ confronted him with what he would do and perform, for he alone, apart from all the disciples, would deny Him three times during His trial. And the Fathers see, in a symbolic contemplation, that the crowing of the cock twice is a symbol of God's warnings in the two Covenants (the Old and the New), and that Peter's threefold denial is a symbol of the completeness of man's denial of God in his weakness, as he denies Him in thought, word and heart. But Peter repeated and insisted on what he had said before, and so said all of them also, that is, the rest of the disciples, in affirming that they had no doubt and wished to die with Christ.

My friend ... trust in God and in oneself in Christ is good, so long as self does not enter into it ... therefore, always ask God's help in humility, and He will support your human weakness, and strengthen you and give you victory in the hard time.
...semane (vv. 32-52):
(7) In the garden of Geth...
32- And they came to a place which was named Gethsemane: and He saith to His disciples, "Sit ye here, while I shall pray."

33- And He taketh with Him Peter and James and John, and began to be sore amazed, and to be very heavy; 34- And saith unto them, "My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death: tarry ye here, and watch." 35- And He went forward a little, and fell on the ground, and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from Him. 36- And He said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto Thee; take away this cup from Me: nevertheless not what I will, but what Thou wilt." 37- And He cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, "Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour? 38- Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation. The spirit truly is ready, but the flesh is weak." 39- And again He went away, and prayed, and spake the same words. 40- And when He returned, He found them asleep again, (for their eyes were heavy,) neither wist they what to answer Him. 41- And He cometh the third time, and saith unto them, "Sleep on now, and take your rest: it is enough, the hour is come; behold, the Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. 42- Rise up, let us go; lo, he that betrayeth Me is at hand." 43- And immediately, while He yet spake, cometh Judas, one of the twelve, and with him a great multitude with swords and staves, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. 44- And he that betrayed Him had given them a token, saying, "Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is He; take Him, and lead Him away safely." 45- And as soon as he was come, he goeth straightway to Him, and saith, "Master, master;" and kissed Him. 46- And they laid their hands on Him, and took Him. 47- And one of them that stood by drew a sword, and smote a servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear.

48- And Jesus answered and said unto them, "Are ye come out, as against a thief, with swords and with staves to take Me? 49- I was daily with you in the temple teaching, and ye took Me not: but the scriptures must be fulfilled." 50- And they all forsook Him, and fled.
51- And there followed Him a certain young man, having a linen cloth cast about his naked body; and the young men laid hold on him: 52- And he left the linen cloth, and fled from them naked.
On a part of the Mount of Olives, there was the garden of Gethsemane, which means "oil press", because of the many olive trees in it.

The Lord commanded the Twelve to sit, then chose from them three, Peter, James and John, who had seen Him in the glory of the transfiguration, so that they would not stumble when they saw Him in suffering and weakness during His prayer and His last hours before His arrest, trial and crucifixion. And indeed, they saw His face with the signs of human pain and distress showing on it.
The Lord Jesus did not hide His human feelings from His disciples, but was frank with them about them, saying:

"My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death", that is, the sorrow reached its utmost within Him, for He knows in His divinity what is coming upon Him. And His human sorrow was a compound sorrow, if the expression is permissible, because:
(1) Christ sorrowed because, being innocent and pure, He began to bear all the sins of the evil world, and what a weight and burden, as He bears all the evil and uncleanness.
(2) Christ also sorrowed because - as a man - injustice would fall upon Him, since redemption requires the death of an innocent one without sin on behalf of a sinful mankind.

And therefore, despite His submitting by His own will to what was coming upon Him and what He knew, He prayed to the Father in His humanity asking that these sufferings be taken from Him, in proof of His perfect humanity.

"Abba, Father": an expression transferred from the Chaldean language to the Aramaic dialect, and it was known among the Jews. St. Paul also used it in (Rom; 8:15, Gal 4:6). The two words carry one meaning, namely "Father", but as one expression they carry deeper meanings of love, familiarity and strong attachment, and to understand it well, we compare it to the colloquial expression "Yaba, ya abouya" (Daddy, my father).

We are still in the same scene with all its bitter feelings and sufferings, as the Lord Jesus lifts His heart to the heavenly Father who is able to do all things, asking Him to take from Him the sufferings of the cross. But He - in perfect obedience - surrenders His will to the Father, declaring His submission to accept it.

Would that we learned from this scene the acceptance of God's will in our lives, and learned from our Savior the persistence of prayer as He did, and did not hide our feelings from God however sad or bitter they may be, and let us trust that as long as He has allowed them, He will help us in them and against them...

Christ had gone a little further from His disciples to be alone with the Father in His prayer, and on His return He found the disciples sleeping, and He addressed Peter reproachfully: "Couldest not thou watch with Me in My sufferings even one hour?" But the gentle and kind Christ, after His reproach, made an excuse for Peter and the two disciples, that their spiritual will wanted to watch and to complete every spiritual work with Him, but the flesh, with its heaviness and weak will, is often a burden on the spirit and hinders its longing.

Yes, my God, for we often claim that our spirits are ready and we give great promises, but the lack of striving makes us carry out none of them ... so let us compel ourselves, even with little striving, and not surrender to the weakness of the flesh, lest we enter into temptation.

The Lord went to pray again alone with the same feelings of weakness as before, and returned to His disciples again. And because of the heaviness of their bodies and their drowsiness, He found them asleep again, and they could not answer Him - out of shame - since He had said to them before: "Watch and pray".

The Lord Jesus returned a third time to His disciples, and this time He reproached them also with His saying: sleep on ... and take your rest, for the time of the striving of prayer has passed, and the hour of the Son of Man has come, in which He is delivered - by His own will - into the hands of sinners and wicked unjust men.

"Rise up, let us go": Christ knew in His divinity the coming of Judas and those with him to arrest Him, so He went Himself to meet them and did not wait to be arrested, for by going, Christ wanted to prove to His disciples and to us that it was He who gave Himself up, and He who knows His hour when it will be.

During this talk, which was the last before His arrest, Judas came (knowing the place) and with him a great multitude of servants and men of the chief priests, scribes and elders, each carrying a sword or a thick staff, expecting a struggle with the disciples before arresting the Lord.

"Judas, one of the twelve": both St. Matthew and St. Mark used this expression to indicate the hideousness of the betrayal whose source was one of those closest to the Lord Christ throughout the years of His preaching, and what a betrayal!!!

The betrayer - Judas - used a sign by which the crowd would know the person of the Lord Jesus, and by a strange irony he used the kiss, which is a sign of love and the greatest friendship, in delivering up the Lord. And in flagrant hypocrisy also, he called Him twice: "Master, master", which is a call of respect and submission from a disciple to his teacher, by which he hides his evil and betrayal. And the words: "lead Him away safely", by them Judas meant that the crowd with him should not make a commotion that would draw attention, and hinder and spoil the operation of arresting Christ.
When Judas kissed the Lord, the crowd rushed upon the peaceful Lord. And in sad wonder, St. Augustine describes the scene, saying: "They seized the One who came to set them free!!"

There were two swords with the Apostles (Lk 22:38), and what is meant by the sword here is a knife no longer than 30 cm which was used for cutting bread, and one of the two swords was with Peter (Jn 18:10), who was appalled by what he saw, so he hurried and struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear. And the cutting off of the ear here is a symbolic reference to the Jewish nation, which cut off its ears from listening to the Lord.

The Lord Christ rebuked and reproached those who came to arrest Him, for this night-time throng looked like an ambush for one of the dangerous thieves, despite His constant presence and appearance all day before the people, and this rebuke is a reference to their real cowardice before Christ, and before the people's attachment to Him, so they resorted to this method. And the Lord also makes clear that what they did is what the prophets prophesied (Ps; 22, Isa; 53, Zech 13:7).

"They all forsook Him": what is meant here is the disciples, who, from the shock of the surprise, were afraid in their human weakness and left Christ alone, so that what Christ prophesied in (Jn 16:32) might be fulfilled, that a time would come when the disciples would leave Him alone.
"And there followed Him a certain young man": he is St. Mark himself, the writer of the Gospel, and he did not mention his name out of his humility.

"A linen cloth": that is, the outer garment. And when some of the young men laid hold on him to arrest him, he was afraid and fled in his underclothes - that is, naked - since he was a young, weak, frightened youth, and he has his excuse in all this, since the disciples themselves fled.

The crowd went with the Lord Jesus to the house of the high priest "Caiaphas", where all the chief priests, scribes and Pharisees had gathered in his house. And it is noticed that St. Mark did not mention the going first to the house of "Annas" as it is mentioned in (Jn 18:13), who was the former high priest and father-in-law of "Caiaphas", and was content with the trial that took place in the house of "Caiaphas", who was the current and official high priest at that time. And of the Twelve none went to the house of "Caiaphas" except John, and Peter, who followed him cautiously from afar, and remained outside with the servants warming himself by the fire because of the severe cold (Jn 18:18).

"To put Him to death": this word is considered the pivot for explaining these two verses, for the trial was a sham, and the sentence had already been decided by the chief priests and elders, that Christ must be killed. And in order to complete this theatrical scene, they called many to bear witness against Christ with testimonies that would justify their killing Him; and because all the testimonies were false, they differed more than they agreed, and they found nothing against Him.

Others bore witness - falsely - that Christ said He would destroy the temple of Solomon and build it in three days, and even in this they differed and did not agree, for what Christ truly said was: destroy this temple, meaning His body and His death (Jn 2:19), and I will raise it up - by Myself - that is, the resurrection of His body also after death on the third day, and therefore their testimonies conflicted.

The council reached nothing that agreed with their wish, so "Caiaphas", the president of the council, arose and asked the Lord: do You not defend Yourself against what these people accuse You of? But Christ answered nothing and remained silent as Isaiah prophesied: "He openeth not His mouth: He is brought as a lamb to the slaughter" (Isa 53:7). And when "Caiaphas" lost patience, he asked Christ a direct question: "Art Thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed (God)?"

Christ was silent and did not defend Himself, when the questions and testimonies were false, in order to bear the injustice of the wicked. But when the question was connected with His person and His self, He did not deny Himself, but declared clearly and powerfully that He is the Christ, the Son of the living God, indeed He declared His coming glory that would be revealed in His resurrection and ascension and sitting at the right hand of Power (the Father), and also His fearful second coming on the clouds (Acts 1:11) at the end of the world.

Christ's reply to the high priest fell like a thunderbolt - when He declared His divinity and His coming on the clouds - and therefore he cried out in anger declaring: (a) the blasphemy of Christ. (b) that he had no need of witnesses. And his expression of his anger came in an act the Law forbids, namely the rending of his clothes (Lev 10:6, 21:10). And by this act, without his knowing it, the rending of his clothes was a sign of the end of the priesthood of the Old Testament and the nullity of animal sacrifice, and the beginning of the living, continuing law of the New Testament in the person of Christ, who in turn hands over the priesthood to the new Church in the person of the Fathers the Apostles, then the bishops and priests.

After this "Caiaphas" asked for the council's opinion, and they agreed with his opinion, and so sentenced Christ to death; and their sentence was not enforceable unless the Roman authority ratified it. As for the assembled Jews and servants, they began to mock Christ in insolence and contempt of His person, until they covered His holy face and struck Him, asking Him: prophesy, and tell us who it is that struck You...

My beloved God ... did my sin cost You all these sufferings and insults?! It should have been I who was in Your place ... but You took the form of a servant, and for my sake, my Lord, You did not turn Your face from the shame of spitting (from the Liturgy of St. Gregory).
So repent, my soul, and do not despise Him who bore all these sufferings out of love for you...

Peter was in the palace beneath, that is, in the courtyard of the palace, where the servants had kindled a fire to warm themselves, and with the light of the fire that made the features of his face clear, one of the maids of the high priest recognized him as one of Christ's disciples, and declared it, saying to him: "And thou also wast with Jesus of Nazareth".

To escape the critical situation, Peter went out of the house into the outer passage, after he had denied what the maid said and disowned it. And as he went out, he was surprised by the maid - according to Mark's saying she is the same maid, while Matthew the Apostle says: "another maid saw him" (Mt 26:71) - and there is no contradiction between the two sayings if the first maid was the one who told the second, and the second was the one who went after him to the porch to declare and repeat what the first had said, that he was one of the Lord's disciples.

Peter denied again. And after a short time, those present declared and affirmed what they had heard from the maid, and confronted Peter saying: you are one of his followers, because you are a Galilean and your speech is like the speech of your teacher and the rest of the disciples. And here, Peter added to his denial that he cursed and swore, to affirm to them the opposite of what they accused him of, and to remove from himself the suspicion of knowing the Lord Jesus at all!!

I fear, my God, to blame Peter for his action, because I find myself at times repeating what he did, for I do not show You in my deeds but hide You, and I almost deny You in the darkness of my words and actions.

The cock crew the second time, as the sign the Lord had set (v. 30). And at this second crowing, Peter's absent conscience awoke, and he remembered what the Lord Christ had said to him, and therefore he wept bitterly, declaring his repentance for the sin of denying the Lord.

Beloved ... there is no doubt that Peter erred greatly by denying the Lord ... but also, at the sign, he remembered, and offered sincere repentance from a contrite heart ... and we, in many cases, may err like him, through our haste, in disturbing errors. But do we have this heart quick to respond to God's calls to us to repent, He who always awaits the return of His children ... grant us, Lord, tears of repentance like those Peter brought in his contrition. Chapter fifteen: the trial of Christ, His crucifixion, His burial

After the trial of the Lord before the Jewish assembly in the house of Caiaphas the high priest, and the council of the seventy (the Sanhedrin – see Mt 5:21-22), the highest Jewish authority, the decision was made to be rid of Him. Since the death sentence was the prerogative of the Roman governor and not of the Jews, they held the Lord Jesus bound until morning, so that they might take Him to the Roman governor's residence and present Him to Pilate the governor.

Pilate's question here, "Art thou the King of the Jews?", may have come from what he had heard earlier about the procession in which the crowds received the Lord on the previous Sunday when He entered Jerusalem, or from the accusation of the chief priests that the charge against this man was rebellion against Roman rule and a desire to set himself up as king. As for Christ's answer, "Thou sayest it," it is a Jewish expression meaning agreement, and what is meant, of course, is a spiritual kingship, since Christ had already declared that He is from above and that His kingdom is not of this world (Jn 8:23, 18:36).

St. Mark was more concise in his Gospel than the other Evangelists, so he said nothing about Pilate's wife, or the washing of his hands, or the details of the accusations against the Lord Jesus, but was content to say that they were many. In the face of these many accusations, Pilate offered the Lord a chance to defend Himself, but Christ preferred silence to speech, that the prophecy of Isaiah might be fulfilled: "He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter" (53:7). As for Pilate, he marvelled greatly at the Lord's refusal to speak.

Pilate was accustomed to release to the Jews at every feast one of those who had been arrested, because it was the duty of the Roman authority to settle Jewish disturbances. At that time the one called Barabbas was bound (imprisoned), for he was a murderer in one of the riots, and he was condemned to crucifixion and awaiting death.

St. Matthew explains in his Gospel (27:17) that Pilate gave the people the choice of releasing one of the two (the Lord Jesus or Barabbas). He set this choice in the hope that the crowd would ask for the release of the Lord Jesus, but these people were Jews loyal to the priests and the rulers, and they feared them.

This verse explains the reason for what Pilate did in giving the people a choice between (the Lord and Barabbas), for he knew the motive of the wicked chief priests, and that he had found in Christ no cause that deserved death.

The feelings of rage, envy and evil burning inside the hearts of the priests drove them to influence the crowds of people who were led along behind them, so that all demanded the release of Barabbas. And when Pilate asked the crowd what should become of Christ, they all cried out: "Crucify him," which was the Roman punishment for the rebellious slave.

Pilate found nothing in all that he had heard sufficient for the crucifixion of Christ, and he expressed this by asking them: "Why, what evil hath he done?" Yet this question did nothing but increase their agitation against Him and their insistence all the more on the crucifixion of Christ.

Here too, briefly, St. Mark passes over the events quickly, yet he did not fail to mention that Pilate sentenced Christ without conviction, but "to content" them, violating his conscience thereby and fearing the riot that might occur (Mt 27:24); and if this riot turned into a revolt, it might topple him from his seat. For this reason he ordered the Lord Jesus to be scourged and handed over to be crucified.

My dear friend ... notice with me how many times opportunities were given to acquit the Lord and release Him. First Pilate gave them a choice between Him and Barabbas, but they chose to acquit the wicked rather than the good. Then another time he declared plainly before them: "Why, what evil hath he done?" in an attempt to awaken their consciences, and yet they did not draw back from their evil, but grew more insistent.

My brother ... we are not here to judge the Jews, but to take a lesson and instruction. The first is: not to make a decision while we are in a state of agitation and anger. The second is: not to ignore God's calls to correct our decisions. And the last is: not to be led by anyone's influence over our consciences, but to examine them well before God alone. And remember that: "He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the Lord" (Prov 17:15).

If I ask myself, who is responsible for the crucifixion of Christ?! In this scene we find that Judas betrayed Him, the religious leaders demanded His death, Peter denied Him, the disciples left Him in fear, Pilate feared for his seat, the crowds were passive and did nothing, and the soldiers mocked Him, struck Him and tortured Him! So what about me if I were exposed to the same situation?! What a hard and difficult question!!!

"The whole band": the Roman cohort was made up of six hundred soldiers, who all gathered around Christ in the courtyard of the Roman governor's residence and made Christ an amusement for themselves, mocking Him. "Purple": the purple robe, or scarlet as Matthew called it, is a red-coloured robe that kings used to wear.

"A crown of thorns": they made from a stem (or branch) of a thorny plant known as "al-balan" a round crown (a cap) and put it on His head. St. Matthew adds (27:29) that they put "a reed in his right hand," to complete their mockery of Him, since they made Him look like the kings. And in their ridicule, they saluted Him and offered Him a greeting as the King of the Jews.

Among the beautiful symbolic reflections is that His garments which they took off point to the casting off and rejection of the Jewish nation, while the red robe signifies the blood of Christ, by which He redeems us and by which He reigns over our hearts.
Notice also the Jewish nation's persistence in rejection, for it had already cut off its ears from listening to the Lord (see the commentary on 14:46-47).

Continuing this sad scene, shameful for all humanity, which mocks its Creator, its Governor and its Redeemer, the soldiers of the band dared to attack the Lord by striking His head in the worst form of insult, and they spat on Him, and bowed down in mockery of the title of King. And after this very painful scene, they took off Him the purple robe and put His own garments on Him, and then led Him out to the way of the Cross.

O my soul ... what can you say before this wonderful scene, beyond description ... who is mocking whom, and why all this, is it not because of you ... is it not for your liberation?! And in return, what are you doing ... do you keep the favour ... or do you still pain Him with your many sins?!

Repent, O my soul, and do not forget the sufferings of your Saviour, for if they remain before you, I do not think you will dare to do wrong ... Forgive us, O holy Saviour ... and we thank You for all that You endured for our sake.

Christ carried His cross at the beginning of the way (Jn 19:17), and when exhaustion overtook Him, because of the scourging, the staying awake all night and the many trials, the Roman soldiers compelled a Jewish man who had grown up in Cyrene – in northern Libya – so that his title became the Cyrenian. It seems that his sons Alexander and Rufus became known to the community of Christians afterward, since St. Mark took care to mention their names.

"Golgotha": that is, "skull," a place outside Jerusalem. Some say that it is a high rock formation resembling a human skull, and others say that the reason for its being so named is the Jews' belief that the skull of Adam was buried in this place.

"Wine mingled with myrrh": myrrh was one of the strong and well-known painkillers that reaches a degree of anaesthesia, and it was mixed with wine – which resembles vinegar in taste because of its cheap price (see the commentary on Mt 27:34) – so that it would be easy to take, and it was usually offered to the crucified to relieve some of his pain, but Christ refused it so that His sufferings might be completed!!

"They crucified him": they lifted up Christ, nailing His hands and feet, upon the wood of the Cross. And the suffering of pain began, and the flow of blood inside and outside His body, as a result of the difficulty of breathing while nailed. It was the right of the Roman soldiers to take the garments of the one they crucified, so they took off His garments – and He became naked who covers all creation with His mercies – and the Roman soldiers divided His garments among themselves by casting lots for them ... in a clear reference to what David prophesied in his psalm (22:18): "and upon my vesture they cast lots."

St. John says, and tradition holds, that the crucifixion was about the sixth hour (which begins at twelve noon – Jn 19:14), whereas Mark, by saying here the third hour (which begins at nine in the morning), means the procedures for the beginning of the crucifixion, which took some time, and it is most likely that the Cross was fully raised shortly before the sixth hour, near the end of the third hour.

It is noted that in Jewish timekeeping there are no breaks between the third hour and the sixth hour, so the end of the first is the beginning of the second, like the difference between morning and noon in our present timekeeping.

"His accusation": it was customary for the crucified to carry with his cross his accusation (that is, the cause of his crime and crucifixion). And since Pilate found no cause worthy of crucifixion, he made the accusation that was hung on the cross with the crucified one: "This is Jesus the King of the Jews," and he wrote it in the three languages spread in the region at that time, which are Hebrew, Greek and Latin. And some add that Pilate wrote this to provoke the Jews, that their king had been crucified.

The death sentence was also carried out by crucifixion on two thieves who deserved the sentence, so they put one on His right and the other on His left, thereby fulfilling the prophecy of Isaiah that: "He was numbered with the transgressors" (53:12), and perhaps in the crucifixion of the two thieves there is an indication that the redemption of Christ includes all the Jews and the Gentiles.

In mockery and ridicule, all who passed by blasphemed at the sight of the Cross, repeating what the false witnesses claimed in their interpretation of Christ's saying that He would destroy the temple and raise it in three days – while He meant His body – and they were saying: Instead of destroying the temple and raising it, would it not rather be better for You to bring Yourself down – if You are able – from the wood of the Cross?! V. 31: Another group of the priests, scribes and elders of the people took part in the mockery of the Lord of glory, and this mockery was intended to prove that what they had done in killing Him was a sound decision, for if He were the Christ – the Anointed of God – could He not save Himself from what He was in now, and they said: "He saved others; himself he cannot save."
As proof of their words in the previous verse, they set a condition that if He were really able to save Himself, they would believe in Him.

"Reviled him": that is, the two thieves who were crucified with Him. Matthew and Mark mentioned that the two thieves were reviling Him, while Luke mentioned the same account, and we conclude from his account that both began to revile Christ, yet one of them did not actually take part in this reviling, as St. Luke made clear in (23:39), (see also the explanation of (Mt 27:44)).

"Darkness over the whole land": this darkness was a miracle by every measure, for there is no total eclipse of the sun that lasts more than minutes, so how then did it last three hours?! It would have been fitting for the Jews to take notice of this phenomenon, and of this wrath revealed from heaven and nature because of their deed, and to take heed ... but so it is with one who is dominated by injustice and spiritual blindness, who cannot see the simplest and clearest things.
O my soul, understand ... all of nature clothed itself in black, mourning for its Creator who bore all our iniquities ... and you, what are you doing now? Examine your conscience and return ...

The darkness continued from the sixth hour by Jewish reckoning (corresponding to twelve noon) until the ninth hour (corresponding to three in the afternoon). And at the ninth hour the Lord Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying: "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?" which means in the Syriac language: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Christ uttered it, and it is the first words of the psalm (22:1) in which David prophesied about all the sufferings of Christ, the casting of lots for His garments, and the mockery and ridicule of Him ... as though Christ were saying to the Jews in a final call: return to your prophecies that you may know that everything was fulfilled completely as it is written ... As for those present, some of them thought that He was calling Elijah the prophet.
Note: it is noted that the Lord Christ, while on the wood of the Cross, had seven sayings, but St. Mark mentioned only this fourth saying (see the commentary on Mt 27:50).
"Vinegar": the vinegar here is sour wine, which has the effect of wine but is sharp in taste, and it was very cheap and was given to the soldiers.

So one of the soldiers took a sponge filled with wine and offered it to Him to give Him to drink, perhaps with a kind of pity, but not without mockery, for he said: "Let us see whether Elias will come to take him down."

"Cried": this was the last cry that Christ uttered on the wood of the Cross, and Matthew and Mark did not mention whether this cry contained words ... but St. John mentions (in 19:30) that Christ said: "It is finished" as His last words ... and perhaps Christ said "It is finished" with a cry, because He wanted to declare with power that the redemption had been accomplished and included all who accept it in the whole world, and then He gave up His human spirit.

At the same moment the veil of the temple was rent, which is a curtain of cloth that separates the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies in the temple, and signifies the separation between the holy God and sinful men ... and the rending of the veil has more than one meaning, as follows:

(1) That Christ offered Himself a perfect sacrifice, with which He entered to His Father (the Holy of Holies), by which He abolished the animal sacrifices and the Jewish worship, and it was the beginning of the New Covenant (Heb 9:11, 12).

(2) The abolition of the enmity between the holy God, whom the sinful man cannot behold except through repentance, and the acceptance of the redemption by the blood of Christ, who gave Himself for this reconciliation.

Among those standing there was a centurion (a Roman), who was charged with supervising and carrying out the sentence. And when the man saw all these events, the darkness, the sayings on the wood of the Cross, and the blood and water coming out of the side of the Lord of glory, he found nothing to say except to declare that Christ is the Son of the great God (God). Consider with me, my brother, the testimony of this pagan man, for he is not of the seed of Abraham, nor was he awaiting the Christ, nor did he know the prophecies of the Jews ... and yet he spoke and bore witness, and his testimony was true ... while the Jews – the called ones – remained in refusal, in stubbornness and hardness of heart and blindness of spiritual insight ... truly, it is the testimony of a pagan by which he condemned every one of the Jews who did not believe in Christ.

Many women followed Christ throughout His life and preaching on earth and ministered to Him in a way whose details we do not know, although St. Luke indicates that: "many others, which ministered unto him of their substance" (8:3), while St. Mark mentions that some of these women followed Christ as far as the Cross, though they stood a little distance away, unlike the holy Virgin Mary, who stood right beneath the Cross (Jn 19:26, 27).
"Mary Magdalene": she is the one who followed Christ after He cast seven devils out of her, and she was originally from the village of Magdala near the city of Tiberias.
"Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses": she is the wife of Alphaeus, who is also called Cleopas, and she is the sister of the Virgin Mary (Jn 19:25).
"Salome": she is the wife of Zebedee and the mother of James and John.

Thus appeared the courage of the women who loved Christ, for fear could not prevent them from following Him as far as the Cross, while the men disappeared (except John – by divine arrangement – so that Christ might leave His Virgin mother in his care)!!!
So it is, beloved ... if the Lord Christ reigns by love over the heart, a person fears nothing, but follows his Christ to the end amid sufferings and hardships.
"Evening": that is, before the Sabbath, which begins with the sunset of Friday.
"The preparation": that is, the preparation for eating the Passover on Friday evening, and also the preparation for the Sabbath, the first of the days of unleavened bread.

"An honourable counsellor": two titles that St. Mark gave to Joseph of Arimathaea. The title counsellor is given to the members of the highest Jewish council (the Sanhedrin), and the title honourable means his dignity, his social standing and the nobility of his character before men. He was a disciple of Christ, "but secretly for fear of the Jews" (Jn 19:38), as Nicodemus also was.

Joseph took courage and did not fear the Jews, but put all his hope in the Kingdom of God. For this reason he went to Pilate to ask permission to bury the body of Jesus. And had the Romans buried the body of the Lord Jesus, it would not have been certain to the Jews that He had died, and consequently they would dispute His resurrection.

Pilate marvelled at the quick death of Christ, since in the punishment of crucifixion the crucified could remain hanging for more than a day without dying. For this reason he called the centurion who had been charged with the execution and asked him whether He had been dead for some time. And when he was assured by the centurion of the complete death of Christ, he gave the body to Joseph.

Joseph bought an expensive shroud of white linen, which symbolizes purity, and wrapped Him with spices and wound Him in linen – and the disciples did not wrap the body – and this was a divine arrangement so that they would not be accused of stealing Him. And Joseph laid the body in a new tomb that he had bought for himself, because the Lord had no tomb of His own, for one who overcomes death does not acquire a tomb, and the Lord was buried in it alone, and after that Joseph and those with him rolled a great stone and closed the door of the hewn tomb with it. And the religious leaders watched the tomb, and they set on it "the guards and sealed the stone" (Mt 27:66).

Beloved brother ... Joseph of Arimathaea reminds us here of an important spiritual meaning, which is that whoever receives grace must close upon it to keep it, just as we place a cloth over our mouth when receiving the most holy Body of Christ.

It was not within the ability of the Marys and the women to stand before Pilate, or the Sanhedrin, or the throngs of the people, but they did the utmost within their ability, so love took them as far as the tomb and the burial, as though their eyes refused to part from the sight of the body of the Beloved until the last moment in which the eye could see it ...

Truly ... blessed and happy is the soul that clings to Christ until the last moment, for to it He says: "He that overcometh shall inherit all things; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son" (Rev 21:7).
Grant us, O Lord, never to close our eyes each night except that Your image is the last thing we have beheld with our hearts ... Amen. From the Resurrection to the Ascension

entries.section: (1) The women's visit to the tomb

paragraphs.text: "When the sabbath was past": that is, after sunset, the women bought spices to go with them to the tomb to complete the wrapping of the body of the Lord Jesus. This is a new proof of the intensity of their love for Christ on the one hand, and on the other that the idea of the Lord's resurrection was completely far from their minds.

Note: Christ spent in the tomb part of Friday, and also the night of the Sabbath and its day, and then the night of Sunday until its dawn. By the reckoning followed among the Jews, the period is counted as three days.

entries.section: (1) The women's visit to the tomb

paragraphs.text: "Very early": this expression agrees with the words of John the Evangelist in (20:1), "early, when it was yet dark," yet St. Mark adds "at the rising of the sun," and so we understand that the women's departure from the city was while it was still dark. And when they arrived, the features of the day were becoming clear, and their thought was occupied with whom they would find to roll away for them the very great stone, which needed several men to remove it.

entries.section: (1) The women's visit to the tomb

paragraphs.text: When they arrived, a surprise awaited them, for they found that the stone had been moved from its place and the tomb was open. And when they entered, they found an angel in white garments, who appeared to them in the form of a man, and they were amazed. St. Luke indicates (24:4), "behold, two men stood by them," and St. John indicates (20:12) "two angels in white." And as happens when each witness of an event sheds light on certain different aspects of that event, it is most likely that Mark mentioned only the angel who spoke.

entries.section: (1) The women's visit to the tomb

paragraphs.text: The angel hastened to speak to them, reassuring them not to be afraid or amazed, for he knew whom they sought. "Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified": it would have sufficed the angel to say Jesus, or the Nazarene, or the Crucified, but he said the name of the Lord and His attributes to assure them that he was speaking of the same Person without any confusion.

"Crucified": he could have said the Risen One instead of the Crucified, but the Crucified is the attribute of love, self-giving and redemption, and it became a title that does not leave Christ even after His resurrection, and a pride to all of us, and a emblem of our acceptance of His love and His boundless redemption.
"Behold the place": the angel pointed to the place where the body of the Saviour had been laid to confirm the emptiness of the place and the resurrection of Christ.

God fulfilled His promise of the resurrection ... and therefore we must trust that He is faithful and true, fulfilling all His promises, for the power of God that raised the body of Christ from the dead is available to us to raise our souls, dead morally and spiritually, to life, so that we can change and grow and live the life of the resurrection.

entries.section: (1) The women's visit to the tomb

paragraphs.text: The angel asked the women to go and tell the disciples and Peter the news of the resurrection and its confirmation, and that they should go to Galilee, where Christ would go before them and appear to them as confirmation of His resurrection from the dead. But the disciples were filled with terror, so they remained in Jerusalem (Jn 20:19, 26), and the Lord Jesus met them first in Jerusalem (Lk 24), and afterward in Galilee (Jn 21), then returned to Jerusalem, where He ascended to heaven from the Mount of Olives (Acts 1:2).

And we learn from this something for ourselves, that it is not enough for every Christian to profess his faith, but he must also inform others of the salvation and the lasting acceptance by Christ, whatever their sins may be, and this the Church teaches us in the Divine Liturgy when we all sing the hymn: "Amen ... Amen ... Amen, we proclaim Your death, O Lord, and we confess Your holy resurrection and Your ascension into the heavens."

entries.section: (1) The women's visit to the tomb

paragraphs.text: St. Mark explains here the feelings of the women who visited the tomb, for in spite of the angel's words and his encouragement of them, human weakness, together with the greatness of the event, caused feelings of fear and bewilderment to take hold of them.

"Neither said they any thing to any man": St. Luke tells us (24:9) that they "returned from the sepulchre, and told all these things unto the eleven, and to all the rest," and consequently we understand that they told no one on the way back, not even friends, except the disciples first.

entries.section: (2) The appearance to Magdalene and two disciples, then to the rest of the disciples

paragraphs.text: Matthew and Luke, together with Mark, mention that Mary Magdalene was among the first women who went to the tomb, whether she was with the other Mary (Mt 28:1), or with other women as Luke mentioned (24:10), and John mentioned that she was alone on one occasion (20:1, 2, 11-17). The meaning is that she was the common factor in more than one visit. And the motive driving her was the deep love for the person of the Lord Jesus, and for this she deserved to see Him with Mary and then another time alone, and she went to inform the disciples, who, because of their grief and the intensity of their emotion, did not believe. And what Mark did not mention is that Peter and John went in haste to investigate the matter (Jn 20:4-10).

"Seven devils": St. Luke also mentioned this (8:2) without detail. But what concerns us here is that God is able to defeat all the forces of evil in a person however great they are (seven being one of the numbers of perfection), on condition that the person humbles himself and lets God work ... Amen.

entries.section: (2) The appearance to Magdalene and two disciples, then to the rest of the disciples

paragraphs.text: Another appearance that St. Mark mentions here is His appearance to two of His disciples (of the seventy apostles). Though Mark mentioned it briefly, Luke related it in detail, and they were known as the disciples of Emmaus (24:13-35), and it is mentioned that they are the two disciples whom, when they told the eleven, the eleven did not believe, but doubted their account.

Here, when the two disciples of Emmaus recognized Christ, they returned to tell the disciples ... so what do we do, having known that Christ is God manifested in the flesh and seeing Him in His repeated visits to us ... do we hold fast to Him, and call people to meet Him in His Church and enjoy the taste of His most holy Body?!

entries.section: (2) The appearance to Magdalene and two disciples, then to the rest of the disciples

paragraphs.text: "Afterward he appeared": the word "afterward" here does not mean the last visit or appearance of Christ among His disciples, but means after the last two appearances that he mentioned (to Mary and to the disciples of Emmaus), for He appeared to the eleven as they sat together, and rebuked them strongly for not believing what they had heard from others about the news of His resurrection.

St. Mark took care to bring out the essence of Christ's message to the disciples as he concludes his Gospel, and for this reason he did not mention whether this appearance was in Jerusalem or in Galilee, but also in his brevity he suggests to the reader that Christ's appearance to His disciples after the resurrection and His ascension to the heavens are one scene (v. 19), but of course this did not happen so, rather he mentioned it for the sake of brevity and summary and concern for the substance, as we mentioned.

entries.section: (2) The appearance to Magdalene and two disciples, then to the rest of the disciples

paragraphs.text: As for the substance of the message to the disciples, it is the preaching of the Kingdom of God, and the redemption of the whole world by Christ and the salvation of everyone who believes in Him. And the two expressions "all the world" and "every creature" mean the commissioning of the Church with what the pure Apostles began of preaching, for how many millions are still far from the salvation of Christ and have not heard of it, and how many souls, after hearing, turned back and drew far from the essence of the spiritual life ... so Christ's commission to us is clear, and the work needs great divine help, with the present world turning to evil.

entries.section: (2) The appearance to Magdalene and two disciples, then to the rest of the disciples

paragraphs.text: This is the only and first entrance to salvation, faith in the name of Christ and then holy Baptism, and this is what the Church has done through time in her preaching, for she delivers the faith and then gathers the believers who received the faith and baptizes them in the name of the most holy Trinity at the hands of the Apostles, bishops and priests. And because of the importance of this sacrament and its standing in the Church, the Church does not accept any joining her and sharing in the rest of the sacraments except by Baptism. And the Church rejects the strange teaching that Baptism is merely a sign, for the word of the Lord Christ is clear that whoever heard and did not believe and was not baptized became condemned before God. And in our present time the child is baptized on the faith of his parents, and from here the parents are responsible before God for planting faith in the hearts of their children.

entries.section: (2) The appearance to Magdalene and two disciples, then to the rest of the disciples

paragraphs.text: With the commission to preach to the whole world and every creature, the Lord Christ gave encouragement to the pure Apostles that miracles would accompany them as necessary proofs for unbelievers in that time, and likewise their speaking in languages they had not known before for the spreading of the preaching.

"They shall take up serpents": what is meant by this expression is that serpents will not harm them, which is also what the Lord had said earlier to the disciples: "Behold, I give unto you power to tread on serpents and scorpions" (Lk 10:19). We may see this happen with the children of God, as happened with St. Paul in a miraculous way when he shook the serpent off (Acts 28:4-5). And the other, more distant meaning is that serpents signify the evil surrounding man, which he cannot face except by a special power that God gives to His children, and they obtain it through their complete dependence on Him and their perseverance in prayer.
After many appearances and teaching, St. Mark mentions the ascension of the Lord Jesus Christ to the heavens (see Acts 1:9).
"On the right hand of God": a figurative expression meaning glory, majesty and power, that is, that Christ returned to His glory that He had hidden from us in the time of His Incarnation.

St. Mark ends his Gospel with a verse that expresses the work of the Church extending from the age of the Apostles to this day of ours, which is going out to preach in the name of Christ, and just as the pure Apostles experienced the work of the Lord with them, the Church – in the person of her servants, her priests and her bishops – still experiences the strong hand of God working in the ministry and in drawing souls to the true faith.

Grant me, O Lord, to be a fruitful branch in Your vine, and a preaching member of Your Kingdom, steadfast in Your Church and Your word, so that I may first be satisfied ... and draw my brethren to You for Your glory alone ... Amen.
